sens: To work for a wage, to be in the service of someone
To worship and honor God through worship and obedience
To render a religious service, to perform sacred functions
To offer oneself to God with devotion and respect
G3000.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is "to work for a wage" or "to be in the service of a master" (the image of an engaged servant). It conveys the idea of dependence and voluntary submission.
2. In the Bible, "serve" primarily refers to the worship and adoration given to God. It is to acknowledge His supreme authority and obey Him: Jesus says, "You shall worship the Lord your God, and Him only shall you serve" (Matthew 4:10), prohibiting any worship of idols.
3. The word can also refer to the sacred functions performed in the temple or for God: the priests and Levites "served" at the altar (Hebrews 13:10).
4. Serving God also means committing oneself to Him with respect and reverence, while maintaining a good conscience: Paul "serves in my spirit in the Gospel" (Romans 1:9) and with "a pure conscience" (2 Timothy 1:3).
G3000.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and originally refers to the work of a servant or a hired worker. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this same concept is expressed by the verb עָבַד (abad), which means "to work" and "to serve." The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) regularly uses this word to speak of the service rendered to God, transforming the idea of simple work into a deep religious relationship: serving God means belonging entirely to Him.
G3000.emploi: The New Testament uses this verb 21 times, primarily to describe the service or worship rendered to God. It appears mostly in the Pauline epistles and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. The word never applies to ordinary work: it is always religious. It is found in three main contexts: the exclusive worship of God (Matthew 4:10; Luke 4:8), the refusal of idol worship (Romans 1:25; Acts 7:42), and the service performed in faith and obedience (Romans 1:9; Hebrews 9:14). The nuance varies: sometimes it refers to public worship, sometimes to personal and spiritual devotion, and sometimes to the service of sacred worship.
G3000.portee: This word reminds the Christian that their relationship with God is not passive: they commit to serve Him, not out of servile fear but out of love and respect. Serving God means dedicating one's entire life—body, mind, conscience—to action and prayer. It is an invitation to break away from all false worship (idols, lies, compromises) to belong solely to God with devotion.

sens: Garden plant cultivated in the garden
Edible herb or greenery
Figuratively: simple and frugal food
G3001.detail:
1. A vegetable is a plant cultivated in a vegetable garden for consumption: mint, rue, lettuce, etc. In Matthew 13:32 and Mark 4:32, the vegetable refers to the humble and small garden plants that Jesus compares to the mustard seed that becomes a great tree.
2. The word can also simply refer to edible green herbs, the greenery that is harvested (Luke 11:42: the Pharisees pay tithe on "all herbs").
3. Figuratively, the vegetable represents simple and modest food, that of the weak believer who abstains from meat and only eats vegetables out of scruples of conscience (Romans 14:2: "one who is weak eats only vegetables").
G3001.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to dig, to cultivate": it is the plant that is determined by digging the earth, cultivated in the garden. The Greek Old Testament translates the Hebrew "yerèq" (יֶרֶק), which refers to both greenery and cultivated vegetables. It is a simple and concrete word, without particular connotation.
G3001.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament. In the first three (Matthew, Mark, Luke), it refers to the small garden plants used as an image of humility and smallness compared to a great tree. The parable of the mustard seed plays on this contrast: a tiny seed becomes larger than all the vegetables. In Luke 11:42, the Pharisees do not fail to conscientiously pay tithe on the most insignificant herbs. In Romans 14:2, the context changes: the vegetable becomes a symbol of moral weakness, of the scrupulous conscience that renounces certain foods. The word retains its concrete meaning but takes on a spiritual significance.
G3001.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus often speaks of the small and humble to teach us great truths. It also invites the Christian to respect those who, out of weakness of conscience, choose simple food, and not to judge them: it is a lesson in charity and tolerance in matters where everyone does not have the same freedom.

sens: Apostle of Jesus, also called Jude or Simon the Zealot
G3002.detail: Thaddeus is one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. He appears in the list of apostles in Matthew 10:3, where he is named between James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot. According to other passages in the Gospels (Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13), this same apostle is called Simon the Zealot. He is also known by the name Jude (not Judas the traitor). His Hebrew name likely meant "courageous heart" or "one who has heart."
G3002.origine: The name Thaddeus comes from Hebrew and literally means "courageous heart" or "brave." It is a nickname given to this apostle. The same person is called Jude in other lists of apostles, and he is identified as Simon the Zealot in Luke 6:15 and Acts 1:13.
G3002.emploi: Thaddeus appears only once in the common French translation (Matthew 10:3), in the list of the twelve apostles. However, he is the same person as Jude and Simon the Zealot mentioned elsewhere. Almost nothing is known about his personal life in the Gospels, unlike Peter, John, or Thomas. He is likely the author of the Epistle of Jude.
G3002.portee: Thaddeus reminds us that Jesus chose twelve ordinary men to be His apostles, several of whom are little known or remain discreet. His example invites the Christian not to measure their importance or usefulness in the Kingdom by the visibility they have in the biblical narrative or in the Church. Even those who are spoken of little can play a significant role in God's plan.

sens: A large Roman military unit composed of thousands of soldiers
A very large number, a considerable multitude
G3003.detail:
1. A legion is a unit of the Roman army, an organized and powerful body of soldiers. Jesus speaks of it to show His power: He could ask God to send "twelve legions of angels" to defend Him, meaning a considerable force (Matthew 26:53).
2. The word takes on a figurative meaning to simply denote a multitude, a large number. When the man possessed by demons says, "Legion is my name, for we are many" (Mark 5:9), he uses this word to indicate that there is a crowd of demons within him, like an entire army.
G3003.origine: The Greek word λεγιών comes directly from the Latin legio, which designated a division of the Roman army. The Gospels, written at a time when Rome dominated Judea, use this Roman military term to be understood by readers and to evoke immense and organized power. The word retains this strong military connotation and overwhelming force.
G3003.emploi: The word appears four times in the Gospels, always to express an extraordinary multitude. Matthew uses it in the literal sense: a legion of angels would be a gigantic and irresistible heavenly army. Mark and Luke use it in the story of the demoniac of Gadara, where a crowd of demons possesses a single man; by saying "Legion," the possessed man acknowledges the supernatural extent of his possession. In all cases, the word emphasizes the idea of power, overwhelming number, and military organization.
G3003.portee: This word reminds us that the power of God is incomparably greater than that of earthly forces. God's angels are more numerous and stronger than any human army. It also shows the reality of the spiritual world: demons are not an abstraction, but real and organized spiritual forces, whose multiplication reveals the depth of evil. Jesus, who speaks of legions as something at His disposal, asserts His absolute authority over both the visible and invisible worlds.

sens: To express a thought or message verbally
To take the floor, speak, express oneself
To respond to someone
To mean, to signify
To call, to name something
To witness, declare, or affirm a truth
G3004G.detail:
1. To say means to express a thought or message in words: the angel said to Joseph not to fear (Matthew 1:20), the servant said to the master that he had gained five talents (Matthew 25:20). This is the most common meaning of the verb, that of communicating something to someone.
2. To say can also simply mean to take the floor or speak: the disciples say to Jesus that they do not know where he wants to eat (Mark 14:12), by saying to the village where to find the colt (Luke 19:30).
3. To say is often used for "to respond": Simon Peter said to the Lord words of devotion (John 13:9). The Bible often says "he answered, saying" to show that the word responds to a situation.
4. To say can also mean "to mean" or "to signify": a word "says" something, carries a particular meaning (as in Romans 15:8, where Paul explains what he means).
5. To say is used for "to call" or "to name": to give someone the name of something (Mark 10:18, where "good" is the name given).
6. Finally, to say means to witness or affirm a truth: Scripture "says" (speaks with authority) what is true about God (Romans 4:3).
G3004G.origine: In Greek, this verb comes from an ancient root meaning "to gather," "to collect," and early specialized in the sense of "gathering words, enumerating, recounting" — hence "to say." In Biblical Hebrew, it primarily translates the verb אמר (amar), which has exactly the same fundamental meaning. The Greek λέγειν (legein) emphasizes the complete idea: it is not just emitting sounds (the role of λαλέω, "to speak"), but expressing a coherent thought that carries meaning.
G3004G.emploi: To say is the most frequent verb of speech in the New Testament: 1,213 occurrences! It appears in all the Gospels, in Acts, in the epistles. We find it when Jesus teaches, when he responds to objections, when he speaks in parables. The disciples "say" it to question or confess. Paul "says" it to affirm a doctrine. Remarkably, to say is also used for Scripture itself: "Scripture says" (Romans 4:3), because the written words retain their power of speech, they "say" something true. Biblical usage shows that to say is not only to emit words, but to convey a meaning, an intention, an affirmation that binds the heart to the truth.
G3004G.portee: For the Christian, this verb reminds us of the power of the word. Jesus "says" and things happen, demons obey, the sick are healed. The word of God "says" what it does. Meditating on this verb also teaches us to weigh our own words: to say is not only to make noise, but to let out a thought that engages our moral responsibility. That is why the Gospels faithfully report what has been "said" — the meaning of the message takes precedence over the mere event.

sens: To give a name to someone or something; to name.
To designate someone by a title or quality.
To summon, invite someone to come.
To say, affirm, express a thought.
To mean, to signify.
To qualify as, to treat as.
G3004H.detail:
1. To call means to give a name, to name someone. When Joseph receives the Child, he "calls him by the name of Jesus" (Matthew 1:25 implicit): this imposes his identity. The village where Jesus meets the Samaritan woman is "called" Sychar (John 4:5): that is its name.

2. To call is also to recognize or proclaim the quality, the title of someone. When David "calls him Lord" (Mark 12:37), he designates him as such, he recognizes him as such. Jesus says to his disciples: "I no longer call you servants... but friends" (John 15:15): he changes their status, gives them a new title.

3. To call is to summon, invite. Jesus "calls" Simon and Andrew (Matthew 4:18): he invites them to follow him, to come to him. It is a call to a vocation, a mission.

4. To call is to say, to speak, to express a word. This is the most common meaning: to state something, to affirm, to declare. Example: "He calls it a synagogue" (Acts 6:9).

5. To call can sometimes mean, to signify. Mark 14:71: Jesus swears saying "that he does not know this man" — that is what his words mean.

6. To call is to qualify, to treat as. In Hebrews 11:24, "Moses, when he had grown up, refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter": he was qualified as such, treated as such.
G3004H.origine: The Greek verb λέγω (legō) comes from a very ancient root meaning "to gather, to collect" and then "to count, to enumerate" — hence "to recount," "to say." The Hebrew verb it often translates is אמר (amar), "to say, to speak." It is one of the most frequent verbs in the New Testament: it expresses the fundamental act of speech. The Greek language distinguishes λέγω (what is said, the meaning, the thought) from λαλέω (the act of speaking, the sound, the physical act), but this distinction blurs in the Greek of the New Testament.
G3004H.emploi: Λέγω is by far the most frequent verb in the New Testament: it appears more than 2,000 times. It primarily designates the action of saying, affirming a word — before a direct speech (Matthew 9:34), before a complement clause with "that" (Mark 3:21), or alone (Acts 13:15). But it also means to name, to call someone: "Joseph, called Judas" (Luke 22:47), "the place called Golgotha" (Matthew 27:33). It can mark a summoning (Matthew 4:18: Jesus calls his disciples), an official designation (Matthew 26:3: the chief priests summoned), or a qualification (John 15:15: Jesus elevates his disciples from the status of servants to that of friends). Its usage varies according to context: it can simply be the equivalent of "to speak" or carry a deeper meaning when it comes to naming, revealing an identity or a vocation.
G3004H.portee: This verb reminds us of the power of the word in the Bible. To call is more than to pronounce sounds: it is to name, to reveal an identity, to confer a mission. When Jesus "calls" his disciples (Matthew 4:18), he does not just emit a sound — he creates a bond, he summons them to a new life. Similarly, when he calls them "friends" instead of "servants" (John 15:15), he transforms their relationship with God. For the Christian, being "called" by Jesus is to receive a name, a vocation, a new dignity.

sens: What remains of a whole after the majority has disappeared
A small number of survivors or faithful ones amidst a multitude
The elect whom God preserves by his grace
G3005.detail:
1. The word literally designates what remains, what subsists when the rest has been removed or destroyed — like the remnants of a harvest after the harvest.
2. In the Old Testament, it applies to the survivors of Israel after disasters: a few men, women, and children who escaped divine judgment (see 2 Kings 19:4).
3. In Paul (Romans 11:5), the "remnant" refers to the Jews converted to Christ at the time of Paul, preserved not by their works but by God's electing grace alone: it is a small faithful number that God freely chooses and keeps.
G3005.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to leave, to abandon," which expresses the action of leaving something behind. In Hebrew, the equivalent word (sheérit) carries the same meaning: what escapes, what remains. This notion of "faithful remnant" will traverse the entire biblical history: Noah after the flood, Abraham after the destruction of Sodom, Israel after the exile.
G3005.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 11:5. Paul uses it to interpret the history of Israel: at the time of the Old Testament, as in Paul's own time, God never saves the entirety of the people, but always a "remnant" — men and women whom his grace has chosen. This "remnant" exists neither by the law nor by works, but solely by free election.
G3005.portee: This word teaches Christians that being elected is never a matter of merit or number: God saves whom he wants, freely. It also comforts the minority believer: even if many reject Christ, God always keeps for himself a faithful people. Finally, it shows that God's election is not arbitrary, but linked to his grace manifested in Christ.

sens: which has a regular surface, free of roughness or bumps
devoid of difficulties, easy to traverse
figuratively: made equal, regularized
G3006.detail:
1. The word describes a smooth and flat surface, without protrusions or hollows. When Luke speaks of the "rough ways [that] will be made smooth" (Luke 3:5), he evokes the image of bumpy roads becoming level and passable.
2. It mainly applies to what is easy to cross or traverse, as opposed to what is steep or uneven. It is a mountain path transformed into an accessible way.
3. Figuratively, the word can express a straightening or regularization: the roughness is removed, the obstacles lifted.
G3006.origine: The Greek word λεῖος comes from a root expressing smoothing or polishing. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew חָלַק (halaq), which literally means "to smooth" or "to make slippery." The same idea is found in the translations of Isaiah 40:4, where the valleys will be filled and the rough paths made smooth.
G3006.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament: in Luke 3:5, where it is cited in a reminiscence of Isaiah 40:4. John the Baptist prepares the way of the Lord using the image of a road that will be made smooth and passable. It is an image of transformation and preparation of the ground for the coming of the Messiah. The context is clearly that of preparing the people to receive Jesus.
G3006.portee: This image of the smooth paths speaks to us of spiritual preparation: to receive Jesus, our hearts must be regularized, cleared of the roughness of sin and pride. It is a call to conversion and humility, to remove what blocks God's passage in our lives.

sens: To be devoid of something, to be in need
To fail, to be insufficient
To leave behind, to abandon
To be absent, to disappear
G3007.detail:
1. To lack in the sense of "not having," "being devoid": a person lacks something when they need it but do not possess it. If you lack wisdom (James 1:5), it means wisdom is missing from you and you must ask for it. A brother without food "lacks" food (James 2:15).
2. To fail or not be sufficient: the meaning broadens to what is lacking to be complete. To become perfect and complete, one must "lack nothing" (James 1:4), meaning nothing should be missing from your spiritual maturity.
3. To leave behind, to abandon: to the rich young man, Jesus says, "You still lack one thing" (Luke 18:22), meaning he must leave behind what holds him back — his riches — to follow Him.
4. To be absent or not present: when something "lacks" or "is left aside," it is not there. Titus must "set in order what remains to be done" (Titus 1:5), meaning what has not yet been accomplished or what is lacking in the organization of the church.
G3007.origine: The word comes from an ancient Greek root meaning "to leave" or "to abandon." It describes the action of leaving something or someone behind, hence the idea of absence or lack. In Hebrew from the Old Testament, it can translate verbs meaning "to separate" (like פָּרַד in Proverbs 19:4), emphasizing the idea of what is left or rejected.
G3007.emploi: The word appears six times in the New Testament, mainly in the epistles. It carries two main meanings depending on the context: first, to lack something (to need, to be devoid), as in James (1:5 for wisdom, 1:4 for perfection, 2:15 for food) and Luke (18:22 for what the young man lacks). Secondly, to fail or leave unaccomplished, as in Titus (1:5 for organization, 3:13 for travel needs). In all cases, the word describes an absence or insufficiency that calls for action or remedy.
G3007.portee: This word speaks to us of our spiritual and material lacks. It reminds us that recognizing what we lack — wisdom, patience, generosity, resources — is the first step to asking God or taking action. It also invites us to reflect on what we must leave behind to follow Jesus, and what needs to be accomplished in our responsibilities.

sens: to fulfill an official function, to hold a public office
to perform a religious service, to officiate as a priest or Levite
to serve in an ecclesiastical responsibility, to exercise a ministry in the Church
G3008.detail:
1. The primary meaning, derived from ancient Athenian Greek, is that of a person fulfilling a public or official function personally. It is a characterized service: the one who exercises it assumes the charge and responsibility. In Acts 13:2, the prophets and teachers of Antioch "served" the Lord in their ministry — that is, they fulfilled their official role as teachers and spiritual leaders.
2. In the Greek Old Testament and in Hebrew, this verb designates the service of priests and Levites in the temple: offering sacrifices, performing rites, serving before the Lord. In Hebrews 10:11, each priest "offers service daily" — the daily liturgy of sacrifices that was his own function.
3. In the New Testament, the Church adopts this language: apostles, prophets, and other officers do not "serve" merely as deacons, but by exercising a true charge. In Romans 15:27, the converted Gentiles must "assist" the Jews in material things — not out of spontaneous charity, but because they participate in a mutual responsibility, a reciprocal service towards the brethren.
G3008.origine: The word comes from λειτουργός, which literally means one who fulfills a public charge (from λᾶος, people, and ἔργον, work, labor). In Athens, it was a wealthy citizen obliged to finance a public spectacle or festival. The word has a very specific civic meaning: a function for pay, an official charge. In Hebrew, it generally translates שָׁרַת (sharath), to serve, with the sense of "serving as a minister or officer." It is therefore a service that implies responsibility, an official position, not mere devotion.
G3008.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always in a context of officers or ministers. In Acts 13:2, the prophets of Antioch "served" the Lord — they exercised their prophetic ministry. In Romans 15:27, it describes the mutual duty of Jewish and Gentile believers, each having a responsibility towards the other. In Hebrews 10:11, it designates the cultic service of priests, the liturgy of sacrifices. Each time, the word emphasizes the official, structured nature of what is accomplished, not the sentiment or goodwill of the servant. This is why the translation "to exercise a ministry" better conveys its meaning than simply "to serve."
G3008.portee: This word reminds the Christian that ecclesiastical service is not a private or improvised matter, but the fulfillment of a charge, a ministry concretely entrusted by the Holy Spirit. By speaking this way, the Bible confers dignity to the service rendered in the Church: it is not about being a servant, but fulfilling a function. It also invites the believer to a certain responsibility: to exercise a ministry is to assume the serious charge, not just to participate when one feels like it.

sens: Linen or cloth used for wiping or cleaning
Garment or strip of fabric worn around the body
G3012.detail:
1. Linen is primarily a fabric, usually made of linen, intended for practical use in cleaning or wiping. In the context of the account in John 13, this linen is used to wipe the feet of the disciples after the washing (John 13:5).
2. Here, the linen also takes the form of a strip or belt that Jesus puts on by girding himself (John 13:4) to perform the act of servitude. It is less a complete garment than a piece of fabric wrapped around the waist, similar to an apron or a service towel.
G3012.origine: The word comes from the Latin linteum (linen cloth), borrowed from ancient Greek. It primarily designates the material — linen — before the piece of fabric itself. This choice of word emphasizes that the object is simple, humble, of ordinary make: it is the basic equipment of a servant who washes or wipes.
G3012.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the same passage: John 13:4-5, during the washing of the feet. In John 13:4, Jesus removes his garments and girds himself with a linen cloth, thus adopting the appearance of a slave or servant. In John 13:5, he uses this same linen to wipe the feet he has just washed. This dual use shows that the linen embodies both the attire and the instrument of servitude: it dresses the one who serves and enables the very act of service.
G3012.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the radical humility of Jesus. By girding himself with this ordinary linen, he symbolically takes on the role of a slave — the lowest in the social hierarchy of the time — to show his disciples that humble service is at the heart of his mission and must also be at the heart of the lives of his followers. This image of the linen will forever be linked to the love that gives itself without reservation.

sens: Small plate that covers the skin of fish and reptiles
Image of what covers the eyes and prevents seeing
What falls or disappears suddenly to make way for sight
G3013.detail: 1. A scale is a small hard plate that covers the body of fish and reptiles, forming a protective armor. In Acts 9:18, after Paul (then called Saul) has a vision of the risen Christ, something like scales falls from his eyes: it is the very image of healing, as if a crust or film is detaching. 2. This image also designates what veils, what blocks: in the context of Paul, it is the spiritual and physical blindness that falls away at the same time, revealing the radical transformation of the persecutor into an apostle. 3. In an instant, these scales disappear, and Paul finally sees: it is the symbol of a sudden illumination, where what was an obstacle becomes evidence of healing.
G3013.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb λέπω (lépō), which means "to remove the skin, to peel." It naturally designates these small plates that detach. In Hebrew, the same concept is called קַשְׂקֶשֶׂת (qasqéset), used notably to describe the scales of clean and unclean fish according to the Law. It is an image of surface, of what is seen and removed.
G3013.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 9:18. Luke uses it in the account of Paul's conversion to describe the moment when his vision is restored. It is a striking image: literally, scales fall from his eyes. These are not real scales in the zoological sense, but a representation of cataracts or the film that covered his eyes after the encounter with the risen Christ on the road to Damascus. The uniqueness of the word in the Bible shows that it is a vivid, spontaneous image, suited to the extraordinary moment of physical and spiritual healing.
G3013.portee: This image of scales falling from the eyes speaks to every Christian: it symbolizes the spiritual blindness that disappears when one truly encounters Christ. What seemed normal — refusal, ignorance, persecution — suddenly falls away like a dead film. It is an invitation to pray for our own eyes to be opened to what God wants to show us, and to welcome the moments when our understanding, our vision of the world and of faith radically transforms.

sens: serious and contagious skin disease
ritual impurity according to the Law of Moses
image of moral or spiritual defilement
G3014.detail:
1. Leprosy is a serious skin disease that covers the body with sores. It is an incurable affliction in the eyes of the people of that time, which excludes the sufferer from any normal life. Luke 5:12 describes a man "full of leprosy," testifying to the visibility and severity of this evil that marks the entire body.

2. According to the Law of Moses, leprosy renders the one who bears it ritually unclean — that is, separated from worship, from the community, and from contact with the clean. Only a priest can declare someone healed and clean (Leviticus 14). Jesus, by touching the leper and saying, "I will, be clean" (Matthew 8:3), performs a healing that surpasses human power.

3. In biblical teaching, leprosy becomes the image of the defilement of sin: a stain that disfigures, isolates, and from which no one can free themselves. It speaks of this condition from which we need to be liberated by the power of God alone.
G3014.origine: The Greek word λέπρα comes from λεπρός, which literally means "peeling" or "scaly." It translates the Hebrew צָרַעַת (tsaraat), a skin disease that the Law defined and classified precisely (Leviticus 13). The Hebrew word itself designates a white, scaly, or oozing lesion, the exact nature of which remains debated by historians — but what matters for the Bible is its terrible reality and its impure character.
G3014.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Synoptic Gospels, always in the context of healings performed by Jesus. Mark 1:42 and Luke 5:13 describe the moment when "the leprosy left him" as soon as Jesus touched him and declared him clean. These accounts emphasize that no miracle of this type was expected — leprosy was considered a divine punishment (Leviticus 13-14), and only divine power could overcome it. The healing of the leper thus becomes a sign of the royal power of the Messiah.
G3014.portee: Leprosy in the Gospels reveals that Jesus has authority over what separates and defiles, and that he breaks exclusion to welcome the rejected. For the Christian reader, it speaks of Jesus' power to cleanse our guilt and shame — not by the Law, but by his word and touch. It is a call to believe that no sin is too grave to be healed by the one who says, "I will, be clean."

sens: Affected by leprosy, a serious contagious skin disease
A person struck by leprosy, excluded from the community
G3015.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the disease itself: leprosy, a severe infection that ravages the skin and limbs. A leper is someone whose skin is covered with sores and scars (hence the Greek image of 'scaly, rough'). In Israel, the Law declared lepers unclean and kept them away from the life of the people — they had to live alone, away from the cities.
2. In the Gospels, the leper embodies extreme misfortune and exclusion. Jesus heals them several times: a man approaches him on his knees to ask for purity (Matthew 8:2), Jesus raises the dead and cleanses lepers as a sign that the Kingdom is here (Matthew 11:5). Simon the leper, at whose house Jesus shares a meal (Matthew 26:6), shows that Jesus welcomes even those whom the Law kept at a distance.
G3015.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning 'scale': lepis. It translates the Hebrew tsaraat, which refers to leprosy according to the purity laws of Leviticus. Ancient Greek initially used it for rough or scaly surfaces; it took on the medical meaning of leprosy in biblical texts.
G3015.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the Gospels, always in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. It is almost exclusively found in healing narratives: Jesus heals a leper who begs him (Matthew 8:2, Mark 1:40), he sends his disciples to cleanse lepers (Matthew 10:8), and he cites these healings as proof that the Messiah has come (Matthew 11:5, Luke 7:22). It is also encountered in reference to Simon the leper, a converted man who welcomes Jesus to his table (Matthew 26:6, Mark 14:3), highlighting that Jesus transcends the boundaries of legal purity. Luke 17:12 mentions ten lepers, of whom only one Samaritan returns to thank Jesus. The word thus embodies exclusion, incurable disease, and the redemptive power of Jesus.
G3015.portee: The leper in the Gospels is not just a medical figure: he is the image of one who is rejected, unclean, and hopeless according to the Law. That Jesus heals and welcomes them reveals his love for the outcasts and his victory over evil and death. For the Christian, it is a call not to judge or reject those whom the world declares lost.

sens: a small coin of very low value
currency symbolizing poverty and destitution
a humble but sincere offering
G3016.detail:
1. The mite is a very small coin, one of the smallest units of value in the monetary system of the time — it is worth about one-eighth of a penny. The Greek word literally means 'peeled thing' or 'thin', an image that aptly conveys the idea of a very thin and insignificant coin.
2. In biblical narratives, the mite represents poverty: the widow in Luke 21:2 and Mark 12:42 puts in two mites into the Temple treasury, all she has, which shows her extreme destitution. Jesus also mentions it in Luke 12:59 as the last cent that can be extracted from a debtor without resources.
3. Despite or rather because of its minuscule value, the mite becomes in Jesus' eyes a meaningful offering: it measures not the wealth given, but the heart of the one who gives, her faith and total selflessness.
G3016.origine: The Greek word λεπτός comes from the root 'lepô' which means 'to peel' or 'to skin' — hence the image of a peeled, fine, thin thing. This original concrete sense (a thin skin) has extended to the figurative to qualify anything that is fine, small, light. By applying this term to currency, the Greeks designated the smallest, lightest coins, like our mites.
G3016.emploi: The word λεπτός appears in the New Testament only three times, all in the Gospels, and always to refer to this small coin. Mark 12:42 and Luke 21:2 recount the same episode: the poor widow who puts in two mites, her last possession. Luke 12:59 uses it to refer to the last coin that can be extracted from an insolvent debtor. Each time, the mite illustrates extreme poverty, but also, in the widow, a generosity that exceeds all material measure.
G3016.portee: The story of the widow and her two mites reveals how Jesus sees beyond appearances: what matters is not the amount, but the sacrifice that this gift represents. For the Christian, it invites reflection on true generosity — not that which gives from the abundance of its abundance, but that which gives from its poverty. It teaches us that God values every act of faith, however humble, and that true wealth lies in the heart that surrenders.

sens: Son of Jacob and ancestor of the tribe of Levi
Son of Melchi in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke
Son of Simeon in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke
Son of Alphaeus, apostle and evangelist
G3017G.detail:
1. Levi is the third son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:34). From him descended the tribe of Levi, dedicated to the service of the Temple and the priesthood. In Hebrews 7:5, 9, the Apostle Paul mentions him to show that even Abraham paid tithes to him, which proves the superiority of Christ's priesthood. In Revelation 7:7, Levi appears among the twelve tribes of Israel, of which 12,000 members receive the seal of God.
2. Son of Melchi, appearing in the genealogy of Jesus reported by Luke (Luke 3:24). He is an ancestor of Christ several generations before Joseph, the husband of Mary.
3. Son of Simeon, another ancestor of Christ in the same Lucan genealogy (Luke 3:29). This Levi is not the same as the first.
4. Son of Alphaeus, he is the disciple whom Jesus calls to follow him by the sea. Mark 2:14 also calls him Matthew (or Matth... according to the manuscripts), and Luke 5:27, 29 recounts the same event: Jesus sees this tax collector sitting at the customs office, says 'Follow me', and Levi gets up, leaves everything, and follows him.
G3017G.origine: The name Levi comes from the Hebrew לְוִי (Levi). In Genesis 29:34, it is explained by a paronomasia: 'This time my husband will be attached to me' (the Hebrew verb יִלָּוֶה, 'to attach', shares the same root). Its original meaning refers to union or attachment. The name also designated the entire priestly tribe of Israel, the Levites, devoted to the service of God and the Temple.
G3017G.emploi: The name Levi designates four distinct characters in the New Testament. First, the son of Jacob, ancestor of the Levitical tribe, mentioned in Hebrews 7:5, 9 and Revelation 7:7 for his role in the history of the chosen people. Then, two ancestors of Christ in the genealogies: the son of Melchi (Luke 3:24) and the son of Simeon (Luke 3:29). Finally, the disciple called by Jesus near the Sea of Galilee, son of Alphaeus (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27, 29), who left his job as a tax collector to follow the Master. This apostle is also known as Matthew, the author of the first Gospel.
G3017G.portee: Levi the son of Jacob reminds the reader that God constituted an entire tribe to serve him in the Temple, foreshadowing the eternal priesthood of Christ. Levi the son of Alphaeus, called from the nets of his lucrative profession to become an apostle, shows that Jesus' call completely transforms the one who listens to him and follows without hesitation.

sens: Son of Jacob, ancestor of the tribe of Israel bearing his name
Patriarch from whom the priests and Levites of temple worship descend
G3017H.detail:
1. Levi is one of the twelve sons of Jacob, the founding patriarch of Israel. From him comes the tribe of Levi, to whom the Old Testament entrusts the service of worship and the teaching of the Law among the people of God.
2. In the New Testament, the lineage of Levi holds major theological significance: the priests and Levites who served the temple in Jerusalem during Jesus' time all belonged to this lineage. The Epistle to the Hebrews refers to this to show that the priesthood of Jesus surpasses that of the descendants of Levi (Hebrews 7:5, 9).
G3017H.origine: The name Levi comes from the Hebrew "Llewi" (לוי), which literally means "attached" or "joined." According to Genesis, he is named after the verb meaning "to attach," as Levi's mother hoped that his birth would unite her more closely to her husband. This etymology already symbolizes the bond that unites the tribe of Levi to divine service in the worship of Israel.
G3017H.emploi: The name Levi primarily refers to the eponymous ancestor, the son of Jacob whose genealogy continues until the end of the New Testament. He also appears in several genealogies of the New Testament: Luke 3:24 mentions a Levi in the lineage of Jesus through Mary, Luke 3:29 cites another as an ancestor of the Savior, and Mark 2:14 identifies the apostle Matthew by his other name, Levi son of Alphaeus, recalling the importance of the tribal link. The reference to Levi in the Epistle to the Hebrews emphasizes the institution of the Levitical priesthood and its place in the history of salvation that Christ comes to fulfill and surpass.
G3017H.portee: Levi embodies the specific vocation that God entrusts to a part of His people: to serve in worship, teach the Law, and intercede. Understanding the importance of Levi in biblical history helps the believer grasp how Jesus, as the great priest, fulfills what the Levitical priests foreshadowed and how He infinitely surpasses them. It also shows that God calls and structures His people according to a precise design that unfolds over the centuries.

sens: one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, tax collector
son of Alphaeus
the one who collects taxes for the Roman occupier
G3017I.detail:
1. Levi is the apostle whom Jesus calls to follow Him while he is sitting at the tax booth in Capernaum (Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27). He is a tax collector, a profession despised by the Jews as it involves extorting money from his fellow countrymen for Rome. Jesus simply invites him: "Follow me." Levi gets up and follows Him immediately, abandoning his lucrative profession.
2. The name "Levi" recalls the tribe of Levi, that of the priests in the Old Testament, but this man is nothing like a temple priest: he is a traitor in the eyes of devout Jews.
3. After his calling, Levi organizes a great banquet in his house to present Jesus to his fellow tax collectors and other friends (Luke 5:29). This feast scandalizes the Pharisees, who criticize Jesus for eating with sinners and socially impure people.
G3017I.origine: Levi (Hebrew Lewi) means "attached" or "joined." It is the name of Jacob's third son in Genesis, ancestor of the priestly tribe of Israel. The New Testament retains this common patronymic name. This man bears the same name as the founding ancestor of the tribe, which is not a coincidence: many Jews bore the names of great biblical ancestors.
G3017I.emploi: Levi appears three times in the Gospels, always in the context of his calling by Jesus. Mark and Luke recount the same event: Jesus passes by the customs booth in Capernaum, notices Levi the tax collector, and invites him to be His disciple (Mark 2:14 and Luke 5:27). Luke adds that Levi celebrates this calling with a feast in his house, where he gathers tax collectors, sinners, and other social outcasts (Luke 5:29). These three mentions emphasize Levi's radical transformation: from a despised and corrupt man, he becomes an apostle and host of Jesus. Remarkably, this apostle does not appear in the official list of the twelve in Luke and Mark; it is possible that he is known by another name (Matthew) in the other Gospels, but the provided usages only concern the name Levi.
G3017I.portee: The story of Levi shows that Jesus calls men where they are, without waiting for their prior repentance. A tax collector, a type of publicly dishonored sinner, becomes a disciple at the first word of Jesus. His feast reveals that authentic conversion creates communion: Levi wants to present Jesus to his tax collector friends and those who are disliked. For the believer, Levi reminds us that no one is too compromised, too rich in dishonest gains, or too rejected to be called to follow Jesus.

sens: son of Jacob, ancestor of the priestly tribe of Israel
tribe descending from Levi, responsible for the service of the tabernacle and the temple
G3017J.detail:
1. Levi is one of the twelve sons of Jacob, from whom all the priests and Levites of Israel descend. His descendants have been entrusted with the religious worship: "Those of the sons of Levi who perform the priesthood have, according to the law, the order to collect the tithe from the people" (Hebrews 7:5). It is through his lineage that God established His system of sacrifices and prayers.
2. By extension, the name Levi designates the entire tribe that bears his name, formed of all the descendants of this son of Jacob. This tribe received a unique responsibility: it would not inherit territory like the other tribes, but would be supported by the tithes of the people in exchange for its service at the tabernacle and the temple. Revelation lists this tribe among those who will be sealed: "of the tribe of Levi, twelve thousand" (Revelation 7:7).
G3017J.origine: Levi is a Hebrew name whose original meaning is probably "attached" or "joined," evoking union or bond. It is a historical name, that of a significant figure in the people of Israel, whose religious role was established as early as the Exodus. The name has been passed down to all his descendants, forming the priestly tribe.
G3017J.emploi: Levi appears in the New Testament as the father of the priestly tribe. In the Epistle to the Hebrews, Paul mentions him to show how Abraham, the ancestor of all Israelites, had to recognize the superiority of Melchizedek by paying the tithe through Levi, thus proving the superiority of Jesus, who is a priest according to the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 7:5, 9). In Revelation, the tribe of Levi is listed among the twelve tribes of Israel that will receive the seal of God in the eschatological vision (Revelation 7:7).
G3017J.portee: The role of Levi and his tribe reminds every believer that serving God, prayer, and intercession are a privileged vocation. The mention of Levi in Hebrews 7 prepares the reader to understand that Jesus, although not a descendant of Levi, is the supreme Priest, the one who fulfills what all Levitical priests announced. His name in Revelation, alongside the other tribes, promises the Church that God's priestly vocation towards His people persists eternally.

sens: Qui se rapporte aux Lévites et à leur sacerdoce
Qui appartient à l'ordre sacerdotal établi sous la loi de Moïse
G3020.detail: 1. The word refers to what concerns the Levites, the tribe of Israel dedicated to the service of the temple and the offering of sacrifices. It is an adjective that qualifies everything related to this particular religious order: the priests, their functions, their rituals. 2. By extension, it characterizes the sacrificial system and the religious law established by Moses for Israel. In Hebrews 7:11, the apostle contrasts the "Levitical priesthood" (based on the descent of the tribe of Levi) with the priesthood "according to the order of Melchizedek" (based on an older divine promise): he shows that if the Levitical system could have led to spiritual perfection, there would be no need for a priest of another order.
G3020.origine: The Greek word comes from Levi (Λευΐ), the son of Jacob whose tribe was consecrated to the religious service of Israel. The Levites formed a distinct priestly class, responsible for the temple rites. The adjective Levitical has become established in the Greek language to name everything that pertains to this order, particularly in the Greek translation of the Old Testament.
G3020.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 7:11. The author uses it to summarize the entire religious system of the Old Testament based on the hereditary priesthood of the Levites. In this polemical and theological context, "Levitical" is not a simple descriptive adjective: it represents the old covenant and its sacrificial logic, which the epistle calls into question by showing that Christ, a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, achieves an essential superiority.
G3020.portee: This word reminds the reader that the sacrificial system of the Old Testament, as orderly and divine as it was, was only preparatory. It invites us to recognize in Jesus Christ the true great priest who has accomplished what the Levitical rites foreshadowed. It is an invitation not to remain attached to the outward form of religion, but to grasp its spiritual reality in Christ.

sens: Rendre blanc, faire devenir blanc
Rendre éclatant, lumineux, pur
G3021.detail:
1. To whiten means to make something white, to give whiteness to something. In Mark 9:3, during the transfiguration, Jesus' clothes become so dazzlingly white that no fuller (one who cleans and whitens fabrics) on earth could achieve such a result — it is a supernatural, miraculous whiteness.
2. The word also carries the idea of purification and brightness. In Revelation 7:14, the robes of the martyrs are made white in the blood of the Lamb: they become white not through a material cleaning, but through the sacrifice of Christ which purifies and makes them radiant, symbolizing their restored innocence and holiness.
G3021.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective "white" (leucos) with a verbal suffix meaning "to make." It is the verb that corresponds to the action of whitening. In Hebrew, the verb laban (from which the same word for "white" comes) expresses the idea of becoming white or whitening, particularly in Psalm 51 where David asks God, "Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow."
G3021.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. Mark 9:3 uses it to describe the transformation of Jesus' clothes during the transfiguration on the mountain — a moment when his divine nature is revealed. Revelation 7:14 uses it figuratively: the robes of the redeemed are made white, not by a chemical process, but by the blood of the Lamb, an image of their eternal purification through the sacrifice of Christ. In both cases, the whitening is not ordinary, but carries major spiritual significance.
G3021.portee: This word speaks to us of transformation and purification. When Jesus' clothes become white, it is the manifestation of his hidden glory. When our robes are made white by the blood of the Lamb, it is the assurance that Christ has completely purified us: our guilt is washed away, our new identity is that of the righteous clothed in his holiness. It is a word of hope for those who feel defiled.

sens: Of white color, like snow or wool
Bright, shining, radiant
Mature, ready to be harvested (referring to fields)
Pure, innocent, justified (in a figurative sense)
G3022.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the color white itself: Christ's hair is "white like wool, as white as snow" (Revelation 1:14), and Jesus at the Transfiguration has garments of dazzling whiteness that no launderer on earth could achieve (Mark 9:3). It is a natural and visible whiteness.

2. This whiteness often implies a luminosity, a supernatural brightness: the white garments of the resurrected and the elect in heavenly visions radiate glory. The Greek word expresses not only the color but the sacred luminosity that emanates from it, as in the "shining" of Mark 9:3.

3. In a concrete agricultural sense, Jesus says that the fields "are white" for harvest (John 4:35): the mature ears, golden white, are ready to be harvested. The word denotes the state of visible maturity.

4. In a figurative and spiritual sense, wearing white garments means being purified, justified, victorious: the one who overcomes will be clothed in white garments, and his name will not be erased from the book of life (Revelation 3:5). Whiteness represents innocence and holiness before God.
G3022.origine: The Greek word λευκός comes from an Indo-European root expressing brightness and clarity. In biblical Hebrew, it primarily translates לָבָן (laban), which means "white" and shares the same imagery: a bright and pure surface. The word has a long history in Indo-European languages, always associated with light and visibility.
G3022.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the New Testament, especially in Revelation (14 occurrences), where whiteness is a constant symbol of heavenly holiness and victory. In the Gospels, it first describes the garments of celestial or transfigured beings (Matthew 17:2, Mark 9:3, Luke 9:29, Acts 1:10), then the garments of the resurrected and the elect (Revelation 3:5, 6:11, 7:9). Revelation also uses it for the hair of the Son of Man, the horse of the rider, and the great white throne of judgment (1:14, 6:2, 20:11). A unique agricultural usage in John 4:35 evokes the whitening fields of harvest. Matthew 5:36 uses it for ordinary human hair.
G3022.portee: For the Christian reader, white in the Bible is never just a color: it is the visible sign of holiness, divine purity, and ultimate victory. When Revelation promises white garments to the victors, it assures that the righteousness and justification that God gives have a glorious and lasting reality. Understanding that whiteness is also maturity (John 4:35) reminds us that God's plan for the world and for us comes to its harvest according to a certain timetable.

sens: The fierce and majestic animal, king of beasts
The terrifying power and strength
The adversity that threatens and devours
Courage in the face of danger
Christ resurrected and victorious
A symbolic vision in Revelation
G3023.detail:
1. The lion is primarily the real animal, the great powerful and dangerous feline: it is the one whose mouth the prophets shut by faith (Hebrews 11:33), and whose teeth are terrible (Revelation 9:8).
2. The lion embodies raw strength and destructive power: the devil is described as a roaring lion seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8), an image of his constant threat against Christians.
3. The lion represents an imminent trial or persecution: when Paul says he was "delivered from the mouth of the lion" (2 Timothy 4:17), he speaks of a serious threat, perhaps his trials or persecutions.
4. The lion can symbolize courage and victory: believers who shut the mouths of lions (Hebrews 11:33) triumph by faith, not by their strength.
5. The Lion of the tribe of Judah (Revelation 5:5) is the glorious title of the resurrected Christ, the one who has conquered and who opens the seals of divine judgment.
6. In the visions of Revelation, the lion appears as a living celestial being (Revelation 4:7), an angel or a symbolic creature of divine majesty.
G3023.origine: The Greek word λέων comes from a common Indo-European root found in several languages. In Hebrew, there are several words for lion: אֲרִי (ari) and אַרְיֵה (ariyeh) refer to the adult lion, while כְּפִיר (kefir) refers to the young lion. The lion in the Bible of the Near East is the classic image of royal power, threat, and majesty.
G3023.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, especially in Revelation (6 occurrences). It is used in three ways: first in the concrete sense, in faith narratives (Hebrews 11:33, where Daniel shuts the mouths of lions), then in the figurative sense to denote a threat or persecution (1 Peter 5:8: the devil prowls like a lion; 2 Timothy 4:17: Paul is delivered from the mouth of the lion), and finally in the symbolic and mystical sense in Revelation, where the lion is a living celestial being or the very image of the resurrected Christ (Revelation 5:5: the Lion of Judah, a messianic title; Revelation 4:7: the lion among the four creatures of the divine throne).
G3023.portee: The lion reminds the Christian that hostile power exists—whether that of the devil or of persecutors—but it can do nothing against one who trusts in God. Seeing the devil as a roaring lion urges us to vigilance (1 Peter 5:8). But the Lion of Judah assures us that Christ has already conquered: he is the true king, the true power, the one who reigns over all beasts and all thrones.

sens: State of not remembering something
Absence or loss of memory
Negligence or indifference towards what should be present in mind
G3024.detail: 1. Forgetfulness is the state of one who no longer remembers, who has lost sight of something important. In 2 Peter 1:9, Peter describes a believer who "has forgotten the purification of his former sins": this refers to a loss of spiritual memory, as if the forgiveness received had slipped from his mind. 2. Forgetfulness can also describe an absence, a moral blindness: one who forgets the forgiveness of his sins becomes "blind" spiritually, unable to truly see. 3. It is a form of negligence: failing to keep the grace received present in one's mind amounts to ignoring it, no longer living in its effects.
G3024.origine: The word comes from the Greek root meaning "hidden" or "escaped from memory" (related to λανθάνω, "to escape"). It denotes what disappears from consciousness, what is no longer seen. In Hebrew, a similar word (מַעַל) also denotes forgetfulness or unfaithfulness towards a covenant.
G3024.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 1:9. Peter uses it to describe the spiritual danger that threatens a believer: one who has not kept the benefits of the forgiveness of his sins present in his heart falls into spiritual blindness. Forgetfulness here is not merely a failure of memory, but a culpable indifference towards the grace received.
G3024.portee: This word highlights the importance of actively "remembering" what God has done for us, especially the forgiveness of our sins. Forgetting grace risks losing sight of who we are in Christ and living as spiritual blind people. The text's call is to remain vigilant and grateful, to cultivate the memory of our liberation.

sens: Basin or vat where grapes are crushed to extract juice
Container intended to collect the must or grape juice
Place of wine production, by extension
Symbol of God's judgment and wrath
G3025.detail:
1. The winepress is primarily a basin or vat carved, usually from stone, where grapes are trodden upon to extract the juice (Matthew 21:33). It was a common and important installation in vineyards: a wealthy man would plant a vineyard and dig a winepress, a necessary element for transforming the harvest into wine.

2. This basin served to collect the must — the fresh juice — that flowed from the crushed grapes (Revelation 14:19, 14:20). The juice would accumulate in the vat before fermenting and becoming wine.

3. Gradually, the term came to refer to the entire process and place where wine is made: treading the harvest in the winepress is to make wine (Revelation 19:15).

4. In Revelation, John uses the winepress as an image of divine judgment: the nations are trampled like grapes in the winepress of God's wrath, and blood flows instead of grape juice. This metaphor echoes Isaiah 63:3 and transforms an image of fertility into a symbol of destruction.
G3025.origine: The Greek word lēnós refers to the basin or vat. In Hebrew, it primarily corresponds to the word yeqev (יֶקֶב), which literally means "vat" or "pit," a technical term from ancient viticulture. The word comes from the semantic field of grapes and wine: it is a utensil or facility directly related to the transformation of grapes. The root evokes the idea of digging or sinking — a carved basin where liquid accumulates.
G3025.emploi: The word appears four times in Greek in the New Testament, always in passages concerning wine and the harvest. Matthew 21:33 presents it as a normal architectural element of a vineyard: an owner digs a winepress at the same time he plants his vineyard. Revelation (14:19, 14:20, 19:15) uses it metaphorically and eschatologically: John takes the image of the trampled grape to describe the final judgment where the nations are crushed like a harvest in the winepress of divine wrath. The grape juice becomes blood, transforming a common agricultural image into a symbol of massive and irrevocable punishment.
G3025.portee: For the Christian, the winepress reminds us that Jesus speaks in parables about the Kingdom using images from daily life — the vineyard was a precious asset. But in Revelation, this word also invites reflection on the final judgment: the trampled harvest symbolizes how God deals with sin and rebellion with absolute firmness. It is a serious reminder that the harvest of human deeds will come to an end, and that God is the master of it.

sens: Empty, absurd, or unfounded words
Discourse that is dismissed as ridiculous or worthless
What is considered as hollow chatter
G3026.detail:
1. The word literally refers to words that have no meaning, statements without true content — like daydreams or delirium. In Luke 24:11, the apostles find the women's words announcing Jesus' resurrection to be "nonsense."
2. It is a judgment of value: these words are not only confusing, they are dismissed as ridiculous, unworthy of belief. The apostles "consider as nonsense" what the women say: they immediately classify it among statements that are not taken seriously.
3. The word also carries the idea of empty, hollow discourse that has no weight or authority. This is why, immediately after this statement, the Gospel notes that the apostles "did not believe these women."
G3026.origine: The Greek word λῆρος refers to chatter or folly; its root evokes the idea of words flowing uncontrollably, like an empty stream. It is very rare in the Bible — occurring only once in Luke 24:11 — and appears only once in ancient biblical texts (a citation in 4 Maccabees 5:10). It is a common language term to describe what is considered gibberish or rambling.
G3026.emploi: The word appears only once in Luke 24:11, at the moment when the apostles learn from the women about the resurrection of Jesus. The disciples reject this testimony as "nonsense" — an absurd, incredible discourse that is refused consideration. This is a key moment in the Easter narrative: the text shows that even those who walked with Jesus initially hesitate to believe in the resurrection, finding the women's message devoid of any logical or plausible foundation.
G3026.portee: This word reminds us that the resurrection of Jesus initially struck the apostles as absurd and incredible — nonsense, a discourse that defies reason. Luke invites us to meditate on this tension: God's power exceeds our expectations and usual categories. It also calls us to examine our own unbelief: do we not dismiss as "nonsense" what God tells us because it does not fit our frameworks?

sens: One who robs at gunpoint, who strips travelers on the roads
A criminal who uses violence to steal
One who plunders and extorts
Figurative image: one who breaks in, who violates the established order
G3027.detail: 1. The robber is a highwayman who attacks at gunpoint. He is the very type of violent criminal who strips travelers: Jesus tells the story of a man who fell among robbers on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10:30). He is distinguished from the simple thief (κλέπτης) by force and arrogance. 2. During the Passion, Jesus is crucified between two robbers (Matthew 27:38), common criminals condemned to death. This is a form of supreme dishonor: to be likened to the worst offenders. 3. The word also refers to one who plunders and extorts, who terrorizes regions. Jesus tells the disciples that he sends them out as sheep among wolves (Matthew 10:16) — they will encounter robbers (2 Corinthians 11:26). 4. The image extends to a figurative sense: one who violates the sacred order, who breaks in forcefully. Jesus speaks of robbers who enter the sheepfold without going through the door — these are false shepherds who exploit the people (John 10:1, 8).
G3027.origine: The Greek word λῃστής comes from an ancient root related to pillaging and booty (λεία). In Hebrew, it often translates גְּדוּד (gedoud), which refers to a band of plunderers. The biblical context situates it in the Mediterranean world of the 1st century, where roads were dangerous and robbers numerous. It is a common Greek word, not a rare or specialized term.
G3027.emploi: The word appears 15 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and once in Paul. In the Passion narratives, it refers to the two criminals crucified with Jesus — which emphasizes his voluntary humiliation to the rank of offenders. Jesus uses it to condemn the commerce in the Temple: "You have made it a den of robbers" (Matthew 21:13, Mark 11:17), reproaching its leaders for having turned the house of prayer into a place of plunder. He also uses it to speak of false shepherds who seek only gain (John 10:1-8). In Paul, the robber appears among the dangers of the roads he has traveled.
G3027.portee: The robber symbolizes for the Christian theft, violence, and exploitation — realities that Jesus categorically rejects. By accepting to be crucified as a robber, Jesus identifies with sinners, the outcasts, the victims of the system. The image of the robber in the sheepfold (John 10) warns the faithful to be wary of those who preach the Gospel for self-interest rather than love. It is a call to authenticity and justice within the Christian community.

sens: Action of receiving something
Fact of gathering what is given or offered
G3028.detail:
1. The word designates the concrete action of receiving, of taking what is given to us. In Philippians 4:15, Paul speaks of the churches that "gave and received" in relation to him: it refers to the exchange of material gifts and financial support between Paul and the Christian communities.
2. In a broader sense, it is the act of welcoming and gathering what is offered to us, whether it be gifts, support, or any form of donation. The word emphasizes the aspect of the one who receives, in contrast to the one who gives (δόσις).
G3028.origine: The word comes from the verb λαμβάνω (lambánô), which means "to take" or "to receive." The suffix -σις marks the action or state that results from it. It is a common word in Greek to express the idea of receiving in all its aspects, from the most concrete (receiving an object) to the most abstract (receiving teaching or grace).
G3028.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 4:15. Paul uses it to describe the mutual exchange between him and the churches: some "gave and received" to support his ministry. This expression highlights a relationship of reciprocal and balanced exchange between the apostle and his communities, where reception is not passive but part of a mutual gift. The context shows that this reception of support was essential for the functioning of the apostolic ministry.
G3028.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the nature of Christian support: giving and receiving are not isolated acts, but gestures linked in authentic communion. For the Christian, accepting help from others is not weakness, but participation in an exchange of grace within the body of Christ.

sens: to a very high degree, extremely
great intensity, violence or force
early in the morning (specialized sense)
G3029.detail:
1. This word expresses the extreme intensity of a quality or action. It reinforces an adjective or noun to show that it exceeds the ordinary measure. When Matthew says that the mountain was "very" high (Matthew 4:8), he emphasizes its imposing and inaccessible nature.
2. It can also qualify a violent emotion or state. When the demoniacs are described as "furious" in Matthew 8:28, it is this same word that marks the peak of their agitation — no one dared to pass by because it was so extreme.
3. In a more specific usage, it characterizes dawn or very early morning: in Mark 16:2, the women come to the tomb "very" early, meaning just as the day is barely dawning. It is a concrete way of saying "extremely early."
G3029.origine: This Greek word comes from a root that expresses the idea of going beyond, of surpassing. In the Greek Bible of the Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew *much, very*, the word that intensifies everything it accompanies. It belongs to a family of intensive Greek adverbs: it is also seen in the reinforced form "even more" (2 Corinthians 12:13).
G3029.emploi: This adverb appears about a dozen times in the New Testament, concentrated mainly in Matthew and Mark. It intensifies adjectives ("very high," "very dark") or substantive expressions ("great morning," "great anger"). The Gospel uses it to mark moments of extreme intensity: Herod's rage before the magi (Matthew 2:16), the violence of the demoniacs (Matthew 8:28), the transfigured glory of Christ (Mark 9:3). In Paul’s writing in 2 Timothy 4:15, it reinforces the adverb "much" to describe how Alexander did much harm. It is a word that thrives in critical or striking moments of the narrative.
G3029.portee: This word helps the reader perceive the intensity of the biblical message — not as exaggeration, but as a mark of what exceeds the ordinary and demands our full attention. When the Bible says that Herod was "very" angry or that dawn was "very" early, it invites us to feel the urgency, violence, or solemnity of the moments it recounts. It is a call to not read the evangelical events as ordinary, but to recognize their decisive character.

sens: Aromatic resin obtained from a tree in Arabia, which burns releasing a sweet smell.
Precious offering presented to God in temple worship.
Gift of great value offered to kings or deities.
G3030.detail:
1. Incense is a white or yellow resin extracted from the trunk of a tree growing in Arabia and in Sabean lands; when burned, it releases smoke and a delightful fragrance. It is a rare and highly sought-after commodity, transported by trade routes from Arabia to the heart of Egypt and the Middle East.
2. In Israel's worship, incense was burned on the altar of the sanctuary as an offering to God, symbolizing the prayers and worship that rise to heaven. The law prescribed a special mixture of incense for the temple (Exodus 30:34).
3. Incense was a gift worthy of kings: the magi brought gold, incense, and myrrh to the newborn in Bethlehem as royal tribute (Matthew 2:11), and in the vision of the fall of Babylon, incense is among the most precious goods of the world (Revelation 18:13).
G3030.origine: The Greek word λίβανος comes directly from the Semitic (like the Hebrew לְבוֹנָה, leboná): these coastal and merchant peoples who were well acquainted with this precious resin gave it its name. The same Hebrew word appears in the Greek Old Testament to designate both the perfume and the cultic rite of the temple.
G3030.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In the Gospel of Matthew, it is among the gifts of the magi to the newborn Messiah; in Revelation, it symbolizes a precious commodity of global trade. In the Old Testament, incense is closely linked to temple service and sacrificial worship. The word can refer either to the substance itself or to the ritual act of burning it as an offering.
G3030.portee: Incense reminds us that true worship is expressed through the giving of what we hold most precious, and that the believer's prayer rises to God like the fragrant smoke rises to heaven. For the magi who worship Jesus, incense confesses that this child is worthy of the worship reserved for God alone; for Babylon, which trades in it, it symbolizes how the world trades in riches without knowing the true God.

sens: Metal container used to burn incense
Instrument of sacred worship to present prayers to God
G3031.detail:
1. The censer is a container made of gold or precious metal, equipped with a chain, intended to burn incense (the fragrant resin of libanus or incense). The word designates the object itself: in Revelation 8:3, an angel holds "a golden censer" on which "much incense" is given.
2. Spiritually, the censer is the instrument by which the prayers of the saints rise to God, just as the smoke of the incense rises to heaven. In Revelation 8:3, the incense burned in the censer represents the prayers of all the saints offered before the throne of God. The act of filling the censer with fire from the altar (Revelation 8:5) shows that human prayers, consecrated by divine fire, provoke God's judgments on the earth.
G3031.origine: The word comes from "libanus," the wood or resin of incense. Originally, the same word designated the incense itself (the substance). Over time, in late Greek, it also came to designate the container in which incense is burned — the censer. This semantic shift (from the content to the container) is observed in several languages and cultures.
G3031.emploi: The word appears twice in Revelation, always in a heavenly vision. In Revelation 8:3, the angel holds the golden censer to offer the prayers of the saints. In Revelation 8:5, the angel fills this same censer with fire from the altar and throws it onto the earth, triggering cosmic phenomena. The word remains specifically linked to divine service and mediation between heaven and earth. It only appears in Greek; the Old Testament rather speaks of "incense" (substance) or the altar of worship.
G3031.portee: The censer reminds the Christian that their prayers are not insignificant: they rise before God like a pleasing fragrance. This image invites us to pray with seriousness and confidence. It also shows that the prayers of God's people have power in the divine plan — they provoke God's action in history. Finally, the fire from the altar that fills the censer signifies that our prayers are effective when they are purified by God's grace and judgment.

sens: A slave who has been granted freedom
A member of the Jewish community made up of former freed slaves or their descendants
G3032.detail:
1. A freedman is a slave who has received his freedom from his master. The term refers to the person themselves, not the act of liberation. In the Roman world of the time, freedmen formed a distinct social category, with a status intermediate between slavery and full citizenship.
2. In Jerusalem, "the synagogue of the Freedmen" mentioned in Acts 6:9 refers to a Jewish community made up of former Roman slaves or their descendants, likely Jews who had been enslaved during wars and returned from captivity. These freedmen gathered to pray together and defend their faith.
G3032.origine: The Greek word comes directly from the Latin "libertinus," which was used in the Roman Empire to refer to freed slaves. It is borrowed from the administrative and social vocabulary of Rome, transposed into the Jewish community of Jerusalem in the 1st century.
G3032.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:9, in the context of the controversy between Stephen and various opponents. The synagogue of the Freedmen is mentioned alongside that of the Cyrenians, Alexandrians, and Jews from Cilicia and Asia, suggesting an organization of the synagogues of Jerusalem by the geographical or social origin of the worshippers. These freedmen, having experienced slavery and captivity, formed a distinct community with its own identity.
G3032.portee: For the Christian reader, this detail reveals the diversity of Jewish communities in Jerusalem at the time of the birth of the Church. The freedmen, although liberated from material bondage, were nonetheless attached to their faith and traditions, to the point of organizing themselves into a synagogue. Their presence also reminds us that the Gospel was addressed to all, regardless of social status or past.

sens: region of North Africa west of Egypt
G3033.detail: Libya refers to the coastal region of North Africa, west of Egypt (Acts 2:10). It is a vast territory that was well known to the Greeks, including the area of Cyrene. By the time of the New Testament, the term could refer to both the specific region immediately neighboring Cyrene and, in later Hellenistic usage, the entire African continent.
G3033.origine: The Greek word Libuē comes from the name that the ancient Greeks gave to this region of North Africa. It is a geographical term of ancient origin, attested in Homer, which remained in use during the New Testament period to designate this area. The name reflects Greek knowledge of the Mediterranean world and the lands bordering its shores.
G3033.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 2:10, during the day of Pentecost. Peter addresses a cosmopolitan crowd of Jews and proselytes from all known regions to celebrate the feast. The mention of Libya, placed between Egypt and Cyrene, highlights the importance of this region in the Jewish diaspora of the time and the universal scope of the gift of the Holy Spirit that extends to the ends of the known world.

sens: To throw stones at someone
To kill or injure someone by bombarding them with stones
To persecute or violently attack
G3034.detail:
1. The literal meaning is straightforward: to throw stones at a person. It is an act of direct and physical violence. In John 10:31, the Jews "took up stones again to stone him," showing the concrete action of picking up and throwing.
2. Stoning is a punishment that can be fatal. It aims to seriously injure or kill. In Acts 14:19, Paul is stoned and "dragged out of the city, thinking he was dead": this is an attack intended to kill him.
3. The word is also used figuratively to express violent persecution and relentless malice. In Acts 5:26, the authorities fear being stoned by the people, which means being attacked with hostility.
G3034.origine: The word comes from the Greek λίθος (lithos), which means "stone." The verb λιθάζω is formed by adding the verb ending, literally meaning "to act with a stone" or "to do with a stone." In Hebrew, the word סָקַל (sakal) expresses the same action and carries the same meaning of violent punishment.
G3034.emploi: The verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. In John 10:31-33, it is the weapon that the Jews want to use against Jesus for blasphemy. In Acts 14:19, it is Paul who suffers this treatment in Lystra. In Acts 5:26, the commander fears that the people will stone his officers. In Hebrews 11:37, stoning is listed among the tortures that the faithful of old endured. The word always denotes an act of hostile violence, whether real or threatened.
G3034.portee: Stoning is in the Bible a powerful symbol of violent rejection and unjust death. It reminds us that true disciples of Jesus may be persecuted as he was, and that faithfulness to God can come at a great cost. These accounts teach Christians that suffering for the name of Jesus has deep roots in the history of the Church.

sens: Made of stone, hard mineral material
Object or utensil made of stone
Figuratively: hard, insensitive, unchangeable
G3035.detail:
1. The word refers to stone as a natural, solid, and durable material. In John 2:6, the "stone jars" are stone containers intended for Jewish purification, a material considered appropriate for these ritual uses.
2. It qualifies any object made of stone. These jars serve as concrete, visible, tangible containers—contrasting with what is spiritual or ephemeral.
3. Figuratively, stone evokes hardness and insensitivity: in 2 Corinthians 3:3, Paul contrasts the "tablets of stone" (the tablets of the Law, dead matter) with the "tablets of flesh," the living hearts of believers where the Spirit writes his law. In Revelation 9:20, the "stone idols" are dead, unable to see, hear, or walk—an image of what is inert and without spiritual life.
G3035.origine: The word comes from the Greek lithós ("stone"), a root common to many French words: lithos, lithotomy, monolith, neolithic. It is an adjective formed by the suffix -inos, which means "composed of" or "made of." In Hebrew, the word for stone (eben) also carries an image of solidity and permanence.
G3035.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. It first refers to the concrete object: the stone jars of John 2:6. It then takes on a theological charge in Paul’s writings: the tablets of stone embody the old covenant, a letter that is dead without the Spirit. Finally, in Revelation, the stone idols symbolize the impotence of false gods, beings without true life. The adjective always emphasizes materiality and often the opposition between dead material and living spiritual.
G3035.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us of a decisive contrast: the Law written on stone is good, but it remains external and condemning; only the Spirit of Christ, writing in the heart, gives life. The stone idols also illustrate the absurdity of paganism: to worship what cannot see or act is to serve an illusion. This word invites us to seek true life, not in what is material and inert, but in the inner transformation by the Spirit.

sens: To hit someone with stones to kill them
To kill by throwing stones, capital punishment
To violently reject or push away (in a figurative sense)
G3036.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of throwing stones at someone to hit them. It is an act of collective physical violence: several people throw stones. In Acts 7:58, the crowd stones Stephen by dragging him out of the city and hitting him with stones.
2. In the biblical and legal context, to stone means to execute someone by stoning — a punishment prescribed by the law of Moses. In John 8:5, Moses commanded that adulterous women be stoned. It is an official death sentence, not an ordinary lynching.
3. Figuratively, the word describes how Jerusalem rejects and kills those whom God sends to her. In Matthew 23:37 and Luke 13:34, Jesus says to Jerusalem: "you... stone those who are sent to you." The image of stones expresses the violent rejection of God's prophets and messengers.
G3036.origine: The Greek word is composed of lithós (stone) and bálló (to throw, to cast). The image is therefore literally "to throw stones." In Hebrew and Aramaic, the equivalent verbs are śāqal and rāgam, both used in the Mosaic law to designate stoning as a form of execution.
G3036.emploi: The verb to stone appears 9 times in the New Testament, primarily in Matthew, Luke, and Acts. It is first used in the strict sense: in Acts 7:58-59, the crowd actually stones the deacon Stephen. In John 8:5, it refers to the execution prescribed by the law.
