In the Gospels (Matthew 21:35, 23:37; Luke 13:34), Jesus uses it figuratively to accuse Jerusalem of violently rejecting the prophets. Hebrews 12:20 cites an instance from the Old Testament.
G3036.portee: This word confronts the Christian reader with the reality of persecution. It shows that the rejection of God and His messengers is expressed through violence — first physical, then figurative. For the early Christians, the stoning of Stephen was a warning and a call not to imitate Jerusalem, but to welcome the message of Jesus. It is also an echo of the hardness of the human heart towards God.

sens: Natural rock block, detached or rough
Tombstone, large rolling stone that closes the entrance of a tomb
Bread, food (by supernatural transformation)
Building stone, element for construction
Precious block or gem, valuable stone
Christ or Christian, by spiritual imagery
G3037.detail:
1. The stone is primarily the rocky block found in nature: hard, solid, concrete. When the devil tempts Jesus in the desert, he says: "Command this stone to become bread" (Luke 4:3), simply pointing to a rock on the ground.
2. The Gospels often mention a large stone that closed the tombs: "she saw that the stone had been rolled away from the tomb" (John 20:1). It is a rolling stone, placed at the entrance of a tomb hewn from rock, which had to be rolled to open or close it.
3. Metaphorically, bread can be called "stone" when spoken of in contrast: "Which of you, if his son asks for bread, will give him a stone?" (Luke 11:11). The image plays on the opposition between what nourishes and what does not.
4. Stones are also construction materials: "not one stone will be left upon another that will not be thrown down" (Luke 21:6) refers to the blocks of the Temple, the elements of the building. It is in this context that the Psalm speaks of the "cornerstone" (1 Peter 2:6), which fixes the two perpendicular walls of an angle.
5. Precious stones are brilliant, colored, and rare gems: "precious stones, pearls" (Revelation 18:12) adorn the heavenly city.
6. Spiritually, Christ becomes a "living stone" (1 Peter 2:4), an unshakeable foundation for faith. Christians are also "living stones" being built together into a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5).
G3037.origine: The word λίθος comes from a very ancient root meaning what is hard and compact. In Greek, it is used for all types of stone, from pebbles to monumental blocks. It translates the Hebrew אֶבֶן (eben), which has exactly the same meaning. The Greek word has been enriched with imagery: a stone can become a symbol of solidity, stability, or conversely, of obstacle and fall.
G3037.emploi: The word "stone" appears 55 times in the New Testament, present in all the Gospels and the epistles. Its uses are concrete or figurative depending on the context. Concrete: the stones of tombs (Matthew 28:2, John 20:1), the materials of the Temple (Luke 21:6), or the pebbles of the ground (Luke 4:3). Figurative: Christ is the cornerstone, chosen and precious, upon which faith rests (1 Peter 2:6). Christians are living stones assembled into a spiritual house (1 Peter 2:5). Sometimes the stone becomes an obstacle and a stumbling block (Romans 9:33), that which one stumbles over. Precious stones adorn the heavenly vision (Revelation 4:3, 21:11).
G3037.portee: Meditating on the stone helps the Christian grasp how Jesus becomes the unshakeable foundation of faith. It is not abstract, distant: it is an image of solidity, durability, real weight. Saying that believers are "living stones" reminds us that the Church is not a vague idea, but a concrete construction, an assembly of living people. It is also a call to humility: a stone has no strength of its own, but it holds its place in the building.

sens: Floor covered with fitted stones
Pavement adorned with geometric patterns
Place where a court or throne sits
G3038.detail:
1. A pavement refers to a floor constructed with cut and fitted stones to form a solid and durable surface. It is a common type of construction in important buildings of the time, particularly in palaces and places of power.
2. The word often evokes a richly worked pavement, with stones of different colors or shapes assembled in geometric or decorative patterns, like that of King Ahasuerus's palace in Persia. It is a sign of grandeur and magnificence.
3. In John 19:13, the pavement specifically refers to the place called Gabbatha where Pilate sat on his judgment seat. It is a solemn floor that marks the seat of Roman power and the moment of Jesus' judgment — a space filled with meaning where a crucial event in the history of salvation takes place.
G3038.origine: The Greek word « lithóstrōtos » is composed of two elements: « lithos » (stone) and « strōtos » which comes from the verb « strōnnumi » (to spread, to cover). The basic image is that of stones spread out, arranged, woven to form a floor. This architectural technical term also appears in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) to describe the royal pavements mentioned in Esther and the Song of Solomon, translating the Hebrew word « ratzaf » which means "tiling" or "paving."
G3038.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 19:13, where it refers to the pavement of Pilate's praetorium, called Gabbatha in Hebrew. John chooses this precise term to emphasize the official nature of the place — it is a Roman tribunal, with its prestigious floor and solemn protocols. The evangelist thus highlights that at the moment of Jesus' judgment, there is a confrontation between the established Roman power in its magnificence and the truth embodied in Jesus. The pavement is not a trivial detail: it is the silent witness of the most serious scene in the Gospel.
G3038.portee: Meditating on this pavement helps the reader to concretely enter into the scene of judgment: there is nothing abstract. Jesus stands on this prestigious ground, before the throne of Roman power, defenseless, innocent. This detail reminds us that Jesus' humiliation occurred publicly, visibly, in places of power — and that there, precisely, in the face of human injustice, His kenosis (voluntary lowering) reached its peak before the resurrection.

sens: Winnow grain, separate wheat from chaff
Reduce to dust, pulverize
Completely crush, destroy
G3039.detail:
1. In the literal and concrete sense, the word comes from a Greek term that referred to the action of winnowing: grain was thrown into the air with a winnowing fork (a flat basket) so that the wind would carry away the light chaff while the grain fell back down. This is a common agricultural task that Boaz was well acquainted with.
2. In the Bible, this same verb takes on the meaning of reducing something to crumbs, to fine dust — as if one were crushing grain until it becomes powdery. This image of complete and irreversible destruction gradually imposes itself.
3. It is this latter sense that dominates in the two uses in the New Testament: the one who falls on the stone (Jesus) will be crushed, meaning annihilated, pulverized. Jesus does not mean that one will be slightly injured, but completely broken, reduced to nothing.
G3039.origine: The Greek word λικμάω comes from λίκνον, which means the winnowing fork, the agricultural tool used to winnow grain. The verb retains the image: from the common and domestic action of the winnower, it retains the idea of separating, dispersing, and then that of reducing to particles. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the Hebrew word זָרָה, which means both to winnow and to scatter (as God does with His enemies or as one destroys a people, cf. Jeremiah 31:10 and Daniel 2:44). It is the evolution of an agricultural image towards an image of destruction.
G3039.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, each time in words of Jesus speaking of Himself as a stone. In Matthew 21:44 and Luke 20:18, Jesus borrows an image from the Old Testament (the stumbling stone in Isaiah 8:14-15 and Psalm 118:22). The one who falls on this stone will be broken; and if the stone falls on someone, it will crush him. The word conveys the devastating, irresistible effect: not a scratch, but total destruction. Both evangelists use this verb to emphasize that rejecting Jesus or being judged by Him leads to complete ruin.
G3039.portee: This word of Jesus reveals both His tenderness and His fearsome authority. Accepting Jesus is finding salvation; rejecting Him is colliding with the one in whom resides God's eternal judgment. The verb "crushed" does not speak of arbitrary destruction, but of inevitable consequences: fighting against God can only lead to our annihilation. It is an invitation to abandon pride and to trust in Him.

sens: Sheltered coastal location where ships can moor and load or unload their cargo
Protected maritime refuge where ships spend the bad season
G3040.detail:
1. A port is a place on the coast where the sea is calm and deep enough for boats to safely dock. It is a natural bay or cove, or a coastal facility, where ships load and unload their goods and passengers. In Acts 27:8, Paul and his companions arrive at a place called "Fair Havens," a sheltered coastal location where the ship can stop.
2. A port can also be a place where ships seek refuge during winter or storms when navigating becomes too dangerous. In Acts 27:12, the sailors examine the port to see if it would be good for wintering: that is, if it offers sufficient protection for the ship to remain moored during the winter months without risk of shipwreck.
G3040.origine: The Greek word "limēn" simply designates a natural or constructed shelter on the coast where boats find refuge. It comes from a very ancient Indo-European root associated with the idea of limitation or delimitation: the port is the delimited, sheltered area where the ship can stay. It is found in many ancient languages. In Acts, it translates the concrete experience of Mediterranean sailors who are well aware of the importance of a good anchorage.
G3040.emploi: The word "port" appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts 27, during Paul's journey to Rome. It is a very detailed text about ancient navigation. The first mention (Acts 27:8) refers to "Fair Havens," a harbor near Crete. The second (Acts 27:12) compares it to Phoenix, another Cretan port: the sailors judge that Fair Havens is not protected enough to spend the winter, while Phoenix, which faces southwest and northwest, seems better. This context shows that choosing a good port was a matter of survival for ancient navigators.
G3040.portee: This navigation account reminds us that Paul, even as a prisoner and entrusted to a centurion, is truly traveling and aware of the real dangers of the sea. The word "port" anchors the narrative in concrete reality: it is not an allegory, but the story of men facing the storm who need a refuge. For the reader, it is also a lesson: in life's difficulties, one seeks a safe refuge—an image that the Bible often uses to speak of God Himself.

sens: Body of freshwater surrounded by land
Place where important events take place
Symbol of divine judgment and eternal condemnation
G3041.detail:
1. A lake is a large body of freshwater, completely surrounded by land. It is a place where fishermen work: in Luke 5:2, we see boats by the lake and nets to wash. It is also a space that is crossed by navigating: in Luke 8:22, Jesus and His disciples cross from one side of the lake to the other in a boat.
2. The lake becomes the stage where the power of Jesus and the dangers of the world are manifested. In Luke 8:23, a sudden storm lashes the lake and fills the boat with water, threatening the disciples. In Luke 8:33, the herd of pigs rushes down the steep bank into the lake and drowns.
3. In Revelation, the lake takes on a spiritual meaning: it is the lake of fire and sulfur where the beast and the false prophet are thrown (Revelation 19:20), death and Hades (Revelation 20:14), and anyone not written in the book of life (Revelation 20:15). It is the biblical image of eternal punishment.
G3041.origine: The Greek word λίμνη comes from an ancient root designating a stagnant or dormant body of water, in contrast to the sea (θάλασσα) which is agitated. The Greek Old Testament uses this word to translate the Hebrew אֲגַם (agam), which also means pond or marsh. It is a simple and concrete word, without moral connotation at first: it simply designates a common geographical location in the eastern Mediterranean.
G3041.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament. Luke regularly uses it for the lake of Gennesaret (or the Sea of Tiberias, the Sea of Galilee), where Jesus carries out His ministry: Luke 5:1-2 and Luke 8:22-33 recount events at the edge of or on this lake. In Revelation, "lake" completely changes meaning: it designates the lake of fire and sulfur of the final judgment, where those who refuse God will be thrown (Revelation 19:20, 20:10, 20:14-15, 21:8). The context transforms the word: from geographical reality to eschatological symbol.
G3041.portee: For the disciple, the Sea of Galilee is the place where Jesus teaches, calms storms, and shows His mastery over creation. It is a reminder that our Lord controls the elements and our fears. The lake of fire, on the other hand, solemnly warns of eternal judgment: it is the clearest biblical image of separation from God for those who reject Him. These two uses of the word invite the believer to seek confidence and salvation in Jesus.

sens: The absence of food that causes physical suffering
The state of one who lacks food, the unsatisfied appetite
In a collective sense: general famine, food shortage affecting a region
Trial or distress sent by God as judgment or punishment
Among the great perils and tribulations of the end times
G3042.detail:
1. The word λιμός primarily refers to the physical sensation of hunger, the absence of food in the body: this is what the prodigal son experiences sitting in destitution when he says, 'I am dying of hunger' (Luke 15:17) in contrast to the abundance of bread at his father's house.
2. It also signifies the state of lacking food: the Apostle Paul lists 'hunger' among the great sufferings of apostolic ministry, alongside nakedness and peril (Romans 8:35, 2 Corinthians 11:27).
3. On a collective scale, it refers to a famine, a shortage that strikes an entire people or territory: during the famine in Egypt and Canaan, 'the distress was great, and our fathers could not find anything to eat' (Acts 7:11).
4. As an eschatological sign, Jesus announces that 'famine' will be one of the signs of the end times, mixed with earthquakes (Matthew 24:7, Luke 21:11).
5. In the vision of Revelation, Death itself rides a pale horse and has the power to kill people 'by famine' (Revelation 6:8), a symbol of divine punishments on the earth.
G3042.origine: The Greek word λιμός is derived from a common Indo-European root found in several languages, related to the idea of lack or emptiness. In Hebrew, the corresponding word is רָעָב (rā'āb, famine), which also expresses the extreme need for food. The word does not change its fundamental meaning: it always describes the physical reality of lacking food, whether individually or collectively.
G3042.emploi: The word is used 12 times in the New Testament, mostly by Luke, and carries several nuances depending on the context. In Luke, it refers both to the individual hunger of the prodigal son (Luke 15:14, 17) and to historical famines (Luke 4:25, Acts 7:11, 11:28). Matthew and Mark place it in the eschatological discourse as a sign of the end times (Matthew 24:7, Mark 13:8, Luke 21:11). Paul uses it to describe the deprivations of apostolic ministry (Romans 8:35, 2 Corinthians 11:27). Revelation situates it in the context of divine judgments, where Death brings famine upon the earth (Revelation 6:8, 18:8). The word thus transitions from the concrete (the sensation, the shortage) to the theological (the eschatological punishment).
G3042.portee: Hunger reminds the Christian of the realities of human fragility and dependence on God for sustenance. It is also a trial that God may allow, either as punishment (as in Egypt) or as an opportunity for communion in the sufferings of Christ and the apostolic ministry. For believers in the end times, famine becomes a call to vigilance and trust: it is among the foretold tribulations, but it cannot separate them from the love of Christ.

sens: Textile fiber derived from a plant, used to make fabric
Fabric or garment made from this fiber
G3043.detail: 1. Linen is a natural fiber extracted from a plant. Matthew 12:20 mentions the 'smoldering wick' — the wick of an oil lamp, often made of twisted linen: this is the concrete image of the word. 2. Linen also refers to the fine, white fabric made from this fiber. In Revelation 15:6, the angels wear 'pure and bright linen' garments: this is a noble, immaculate fabric that evokes purity and holiness. This white linen then becomes a symbol of divine justice and holiness.
G3043.origine: The Greek word λίνον (linon) comes from a very ancient root shared by several Indo-European languages. In Hebrew, the plant is called פִּשְׁתָּה (pishtah), from which linen was known in Egypt and the Middle East since antiquity. The Greek word simply and faithfully translates this ancient Semitic term. The fiber itself evokes fineness and whiteness: two qualities that make linen a biblical symbol of purity.
G3043.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, always in significant contexts. First in Matthew 12:20, where Jesus 'will not break the bruised reed' and 'will not extinguish the smoldering wick' — the burning linen wick illustrates Jesus' tenderness towards the weak. Then in Revelation 15:6, where the angels clothed in pure linen represent heavenly holiness. These two passages show that linen, a simple and common material, becomes in the Bible a sign of divine gentleness and holy purity.
G3043.portee: Linen teaches us two contrasting lessons: first, the fragile fiber of the wick reminds us that Jesus treats the wounded and the weak with extreme tenderness, without crushing them. Secondly, the white linen garment of the angels speaks to us of the glorious holiness to which God calls us. Between fragility and purity, linen becomes the biblical image of a divine justice that is both gentle and immaculate.

sens: Christian from Rome who greets Timothy
G3044.detail: Linus is a man mentioned in Paul's letter to Timothy, among the faithful from Rome who send their greetings (2 Timothy 4:21). He is listed alongside Eubulus, Pudens, and Claudia, companions of Paul at the end of his ministry. No additional biographical details are provided by the Bible.
G3044.origine: The name Linus is of Greek or Latin origin. In Greco-Roman mythology, Linos was a legendary musician, son of Apollo, but the Linus of the New Testament is a historical figure, a faithful member of the early Church in Rome. No connection with mythology is established by the biblical text.
G3044.emploi: Linus is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 4:21. Paul, writing to his young disciple Timothy shortly before his martyrdom, conveys the greetings of several Christians present with him in Rome. Linus is part of this group of faithful who support the apostle in his final days. The context suggests that he was an influential member of the Church in Rome, alongside other figures like Pudens and Claudia.

sens: Rich, creamy, high in fat
Providing an easy and pleasant, luxurious life
Precious and desirable
G3045.detail:
1. The word primarily describes what is rich or creamy, like a food high in fat. In the Old Testament, it is applied to fertile and abundant lands (in Greek, it translates the Hebrew word meaning 'fat'), which produce generous and satisfying food.

2. Figuratively, it denotes a life of comfort, luxury, and pleasure — the sweet life of one who has everything they desire. It conveys the idea of opulence and delicacies: the fine and sought-after dishes that only the wealthy can afford.

3. Finally, the word evokes what is precious, desirable, that which one regrets losing. In Revelation 18:14, the 'delicacies' of Babylon — its fruits, its treasures — represent all that was coveted and appreciated in this system of fleeting wealth.
G3045.origine: The word comes from the Greek *lipos*, meaning 'fat' or 'grease'. The adjective *liparos* naturally derives from it: it qualifies what is rich, containing a lot of fat. In the Greek Old Testament, it regularly translates the Hebrew word *shamen* (fat), applied to fertile lands or abundant products. The link between physical fat and luxury, between material abundance and delicious life, is thus rooted in the primitive image of the word.
G3045.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Revelation 18:14. John enumerates what the great city of Babylon ardently desired — its fruits, its treasures, its 'delicious and magnificent things' — to say that all this will be taken away from her. The context is a divine judgment: the luxurious wealth and pleasures that are eagerly sought will disappear. In Revelation, the word thus embodies the seduction of earthly opulence and the illusion of its duration.
G3045.portee: This word reminds us that the pleasures and riches of this world, however pleasant they may seem, will not last. For the believer, it is a call not to set their heart on the 'delicious things' that are perishable, but on what is eternal. Babylon loses what she cherished most — this is the fate of all that is based only on flesh and gold.

sens: Unit of weight corresponding to approximately 327 grams
Quantity measured according to this unit
G3046.detail:
1. The pound is a unit of weight used in the ancient Greco-Roman world. It is roughly equivalent to 327 grams. This is the weight of a costly perfume that Mary pours on Jesus' feet in Bethany (John 12:3), and also the weight of the mixture of myrrh and aloes that Nicodemus brings for Jesus' burial (John 19:39: "a hundred pounds").
2. By extension, the term refers to any quantity measured according to this unit of weight. In John, it serves to specify the value or abundance of a gift: a single pound of pure nard expresses Mary's generosity, while a hundred pounds of spices express the honor given to Jesus' body.
G3046.origine: The Greek word λίτρα comes from the Latin "libra," which designated both a unit of weight and a currency. In the Greco-Roman world, this measure was commonly used to weigh precious objects, aromatics, and spices. The term has retained its concrete meaning of weight, without notable metaphorical development.
G3046.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, exclusively in John. In John 12:3, it quantifies the costly pure nard perfume used by Mary to anoint Jesus: a single pound, but very precious. In John 19:39, it measures the massive quantity of spices used to prepare Jesus' body for burial: a hundred pounds. These two uses illustrate how John employs this term to emphasize either the intensity of the act of love (a concentrated pound) or the magnitude of the funeral honor (a hundred abundant pounds).
G3046.portee: This word invites the reader to concretely measure the extent of acts of devotion and honor toward Jesus. Mary's pound of perfume symbolizes a concentrated and costly love; Nicodemus' hundred pounds testify that even secret figures of faith recognize Christ's royalty. These concrete measures make the narratives vivid and remind us that Jesus' honor is manifested through tangible acts.

sens: The wind blowing from the southwest
The direction of southwest
The region or area located to the southwest
G3047.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the wind blowing from the southwest, particularly in the Mediterranean region. In Acts 27:12, during Paul's journey to Rome, they seek a port that "faces southwest": it is this wind they want to avoid or seek depending on the sailing conditions.
2. By extension, it applies to the direction itself, which lies between south and west. It is a precise geographical direction, important for the orientation of ships and locations.
3. More broadly, it can refer to the region or area extending toward the southwest, as when one speaks of "the coast that faces southwest."
4. In Crete, where Paul travels, ports had vital importance: some offered protection against winds from various directions. The southwest was a crucial direction for assessing the quality of an anchorage.
G3047.origine: The Greek word λίψ (lips) is very ancient. It likely comes from a root that evokes the idea of heat or sirocco, the hot wind from the south. In the Old Testament, translated into Greek, this word primarily renders the Hebrew נֶגֶב (negev, literally "the dry, the parched"), which designates the arid south of Palestine. It also translates תֵּימָן (teman, the south) and מַעֲרָב (ma'arab, the west). The connection with heat and dryness shows that the south was associated with the dry and burning wind in the Mediterranean.
G3047.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:12, during the account of Paul's shipwreck. Luke uses this technical term to describe the orientation of a port in Crete: "Phoenix, a port of Crete that faces southwest." It is a term of navigation and maritime geography. Its use is precise and concrete: one must find a well-oriented port to winter safely. This detail shows that Luke, the author of Acts, had a good understanding of the realities of ancient navigation.
G3047.portee: This word reminds us that the apostles traveled by sea and faced real risks. The precise mention of the southwest shows that God guides His people through the concrete details of life — including storms, ports, and wind directions. It is a modest example of divine providence that watches over every aspect of our journey.

sens: Action of gathering donations or offerings
Set of collected donations
Voluntary contribution made by each believer
G3048.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the concrete action of gathering: one collects by going from house to house or inviting everyone to bring. Paul speaks of the "collection" for the saints in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1), an organized action among the churches to assist poor believers.
2. It also refers to the totality of the gathered donations: what each person has set aside constitutes the collection. The word encompasses both the process and its result.
3. Each personal contribution is a part of the collection: "Let each of you set aside on the first day of the week what he can" (1 Corinthians 16:2) — each gives according to his means to support this common collection.
G3048.origine: The word comes from the verb "to collect" (λογεύω), which literally means "to gather." The root refers to the idea of collecting, putting together what was scattered. It is a practical word, common in administrative and commercial documents of the Greek world.
G3048.emploi: Paul uses this term twice in his first letter to the Corinthians, in chapter 16, to refer to a collection organized for the saints in Jerusalem who are going through a difficult time. He provides the details: each sets aside on the first day of the week, according to his means. This collection is an act of communion and solidarity among the churches — it is a concrete expression of brotherly love.
G3048.portee: The collection teaches us that generosity toward brothers in need is an organized and regular Christian duty, not an improvisation. It also shows that everyone, according to their means, can contribute to this common work: there is no minimum requirement, but an invitation to give willingly. It is a beautiful image of the Church as a body that helps one another.

sens: Count, enumerate in a numerical calculation
Take into account, consider something
Attribute an action, quality, or responsibility to someone
Evaluate, estimate the value or importance of something
Judge, form an opinion about something or someone
Propose to do something, decide
G3049.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of calculation: counting things or enumerating them (Mark 15:28, "He was counted among the transgressors," meaning counted among them). It is an act of accounting or record-keeping.

2. Taking into account means considering something in a judgment or decision. For example, in 2 Corinthians 3:5, Paul says that we should not "think" (believe that we are capable by ourselves): we must take into account our real limitations.

3. To impute is to attribute to someone an action, a merit, or a fault — the most important meaning in biblical theology. In Romans 4:3, Abraham's faith "was credited to him as righteousness": God credited Abraham with righteousness, attributing to him a merit that he did not possess through his works.

4. To estimate is to evaluate the importance or value of something. In Romans 8:18, Paul "considers that the sufferings of the present time" cannot be compared to the future glory: he weighs the two realities and concludes that one surpasses the other.

5. To judge or "think" refers to the act of forming an opinion: in 2 Corinthians 12:6, Paul refrains from boasting, for fear that others might have an exaggerated "opinion" of him based on what they see or hear.

6. To propose or decide means to form an intention to act. This is the meaning closest to the future or will.
G3049.origine: The word comes from λόγος (logos), which means "word" and "reason, calculation, reasoning." Literally, logizomai means "to reason from the word," or "to calculate by reason." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this verb mostly translates חָשַׁב (chashab), which means "to think, calculate, invent." The Greek family also includes λόγος (the word), λόγιον (the little word, the oracle), and διαλογίζομαι (to discuss, deliberate).
G3049.emploi: The verb appears 40 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul (Romans, Corinthians, Galatians). In the Epistle to the Romans, particularly in 4:3-24, Paul uses logizomai to explain how God imputed righteousness to Abraham: it is a divine act of credit or attribution, not a natural reality. The word also extends to the act of judging or evaluating humanly: in 1 Corinthians 13:5, Paul says that love "does not think evil" (does not count, does not record offenses). In Romans 8:18, it refers to personal opinion, subjective appreciation. The verb can thus oscillate between a legal sense (imputing responsibility) and a sense closer to conscience (judging, thinking, supposing).
G3049.portee: This word raises a decisive question in Christian theology: how does God judge us? By imputing righteousness to Abraham without his works (Romans 4), God teaches us that our forgiveness rests on an act of divine credit, not on our merits. For the believer's life, the word also invites reflection: do not "count" sins (2 Corinthians 5:19 — in the context of reconciliation), consider your present sufferings in light of eternal glory (Romans 8:18), and judge yourself with clarity, without overestimating yourself. The word roots Christian righteousness in God's gracious decision, not in human performance.

sens: In accordance with reason, intelligence
Spiritual, immaterial, belonging to the spirit rather than to matter
G3050.detail:
1. The word describes what is in accordance with reason and intelligence, what is rational and sensible. In Romans 12:1, Paul invites believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice: this sacrifice is "reasonable," meaning it corresponds to a logical and intelligent response to God's mercies, not to a blind or superstitious obligation.

2. In a spiritual context, the word takes on a deeper nuance: it designates what pertains to the spirit and divine life, not to mere matter or the fleshly body. In 1 Peter 2:2, "the pure spiritual milk" is not a physical food, but a nourishment for the soul — the word of God — that nourishes the believer in faith and spiritual growth.
G3050.origine: The word comes from the Greek "logos" (λόγος), which means both "word," "reason," and "intelligence." The suffix "-ikos" (-ικός) makes it an adjective. It is a word from the Greek family of reason and rational discourse. In the Bible, this word translates the biblical idea of a reaction or offering that engages intelligence and will, not just actions.
G3050.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 12:1, it qualifies the worship or service rendered to God: it is a "reasonable" sacrifice because it responds intelligently to the divine grace received. In 1 Peter 2:2, it characterizes spiritual milk: it means here what is immaterial, belonging to the realm of the spirit. In these two uses, the word emphasizes that the Christian life engages the whole person — body, mind, and spirit — in a coherent and God-oriented way.
G3050.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith is not a matter of instinct or superstition, but that it engages reason and reflection. Offering one's body as a reasonable sacrifice means that the Christian reflects on what he does and why: it is a conscious and intelligent decision. Similarly, seeking spiritual milk means intentionally nourishing one's inner life through the word of God, accepting that this nourishment acts on the immaterial order of our being.

sens: Word or revelation from God
Divine teaching entrusted to a people
Prophetic or sacred declaration
G3051.detail:
1. An oracle is a word that God addresses directly, a divine revelation. This is what Moses received at Mount Sinai (Acts 7:38): the living oracles that contained the Law and the will of God.
2. It is also the entirety of divine revelations entrusted to Israel. Paul reminds that the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God: it is a privilege and a responsibility (Romans 3:2).
3. More broadly, these are the words and teachings of God addressed to His people throughout time, which one must progress in understanding (Hebrews 5:12). The New Testament itself contains the oracles of God to preach (1 Peter 4:11).
G3051.origine: The word comes from the Greek logos (word) with a diminutive that emphasizes the precious and solemn nature of the word. In Hebrew, it translates words like imra (word) and amar (to say), used to designate the words of God in the Psalms and the Prophets. It is a rare word that distinguishes divine words as something sacred and authentic.
G3051.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always to designate words of God. In Paul and Peter, it refers to the heritage of Israel: the revelations that God has given to His people. In the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews, it describes the progressive teaching that believers must acquire, like children learning the basics. The word always carries authority: these are not ordinary words, but words that God has entrusted and that disciples must learn, live, and pass on.
G3051.portee: The word shows that the Word of God is not an abstraction: it is something living and precise, received with responsibility. For the Christian, this reminds us that knowing the Bible means holding in our hands the very oracles of God, and that this gift calls for growth in faith and obedience, as well as faithful transmission to others.

sens: who speaks with ease and persuasion
who expresses ideas well with skillful words
G3052.detail:
1. The word describes someone who possesses the gift of speaking well, with fluency and grace. It refers to a speaker who captivates their audience through the quality of their expression. Apollos is presented this way in Acts 18:24: "A Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, an eloquent man and well-versed in the Scriptures, came to Ephesus" — he was recognized for his speaking talent and knowledge of the sacred texts.
2. By extension, the word can also evoke learning and culture: an eloquent person is generally someone who has studied and is educated. For Apollos, eloquence goes hand in hand with his mastery of the Scriptures, forming a combination of intellectual and oratorical qualities.
G3052.origine: The word comes from "logos" (λόγος), which means "word" or "speech." The adjective "eloquent" thus describes one who is familiar with words, who knows how to handle them skillfully. In classical ancient Greece, the word could simply mean "learned" or "educated"; but by the time of the New Testament, it had specialized to primarily denote the ability to speak well and persuade through words.
G3052.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 18:24, to describe Apollos. The apostle Luke uses it to emphasize that this man was not only a believer in Jesus but also a quality speaker, capable of defending the faith with elegance and conviction. This detail shows that God also uses natural talents — the gift of speech — to serve His kingdom, even though Paul will later remind us that eloquence alone is not enough without the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:1-4).
G3052.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize that God values natural abilities and acquired talents as well. Apollos embodies a cultivated and gifted believer, able to communicate the Gospel with clarity and persuasion. However, the biblical context reminds us that the eloquence of human wisdom must be coupled with the power of the Spirit to truly transform hearts.

sens: Activity of the mind that reasons and reflects
Personal idea or conviction that arises from this reflection
Inner judgment on right and wrong
G3053.detail:
1. The word designates the act of thinking, the process by which the mind examines, weighs, and reasons about a question. In Romans 2:15, the thoughts of the Gentiles "accusing or defending themselves alternately" show this spirit in action: it evaluates, it judges internally.
2. It is also the fruit of this reflection: the idea or conviction that forms in a person's heart. When Paul speaks of thoughts that testify, he refers to the judgments, the conclusions that the mind has reached.
3. In particular, it is the moral judgment: the thought by which the soul discerns right from wrong, approves or condemns its own actions. This inner judgment is what Paul calls the conscience in action.
G3053.origine: The word comes from the verb "logizesthai" (to count, calculate, reason). Originally, it evokes the image of a calculation, an account to be made — like one does in a commercial calculation. From there, it has shifted to the general idea of reasoning and thought. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates "mahashavah," which designates both the plan and the thought, the intention of the heart.
G3053.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek Bible in the attested uses (Romans 2:15). Paul uses it to describe how the conscience of the Gentiles functions: it emits thoughts, judgments that accuse or defend. It is a term that fits the context of Paul's argumentation on the natural law inscribed in the heart: the thoughts are the voices of this inner law that judges.
G3053.portee: This word shows that everyone carries within themselves a capacity for moral judgment, a place where the truth of right and wrong is heard. The thoughts that accuse or defend reveal that we cannot escape the inner verdict: we know, deep down, when we transgress. It is a word of responsibility and hope — responsibility because we judge ourselves; hope because this inner light is a sign of God's presence.

sens: To quarrel or dispute using words rather than substance
To engage in a futile argument about the meaning or form of words, without real stakes
To waste time and energy in verbose arguments devoid of spiritual value
G3054.detail:
1. The word literally describes the struggle (μάχη) waged by words (λόγος) — that is, a quarrel, a dispute where one confronts mainly through words. In 2 Timothy 2:14, Paul urges Timothy to remind the faithful to "avoid disputes of words": he speaks of those verbal jousts where one debates the exact meaning of a term rather than the truth itself.
2. It is a hollow quarrel, without solid foundation — it shines through rhetoric or skill in handling words, but it builds nothing and saves no one. That is why Paul adds that it "only serves to ruin those who listen": instead of edifying faith, it undermines it.
3. The image is that of a sterile fight, where one exchanges verbal blows instead of moving toward truth and life. It is wasting time and that of others in quibbles rather than serving the Gospel with clarity and simplicity.
G3054.origine: The word is composed of λόγος (word, speech) and μάχομαι (to fight, to quarrel). It literally designates a battle of words — the very form of the French word "logomachia" retains this image. In Hebrew, this type of futile quarrel would be close to the notion of "vain debate" that the Old Testament also condemns. It is a rare word, attested only once in the New Testament.
G3054.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Timothy 2:14. Paul, in his letter to young Timothy, uses it to warn him against a practice that has become common in churches: Byzantine disputes over words. It is not about legitimate theological debate, but a form of intellectual vanity where one takes pleasure in arguing, quarreling over terms, without concern for truth or the edification of souls. It is in the pastoral context: Timothy must protect the flock from these sterile quarrels that divide and mislead it.
G3054.portee: This word invites the reader to discern the difference between a genuine questioning of faith and a mere dispute of words. For the Christian, it is a call to flee intellectual vanity and seek a true understanding of the Gospel, rather than indulging in fruitless debates. It is also a warning: words carry weight, they can wound or edify; one who delights in "logomachia" risks ruining the faith of those who listen. Sobriety and clarity of language in service of the truth are the antidote to this evil.

sens: quarrel over words rather than facts
sterile debate focused on form rather than substance
vain discussion motivated by pride rather than the pursuit of truth
G3055.detail:
1. A dispute of words is a quarrel where one fights not over the things themselves, but over the way they are said or named. The Greek word combines "logos" (the word, reason) and "machia" (combat). It is a verbal confrontation where the disputants seek to be right through talk rather than through truth: they quibble over words.
2. It is a debate that goes nowhere, benefiting no one. In 1 Timothy 6:4, Paul describes a man "puffed up with pride" who "has a morbid craving for controversy and for disputes about words": he loves to argue for the sake of arguing, to show off his knowledge or rhetorical skill, without seeking to edify or enlighten.
3. This quarrel arises from pride and self-love, not from love of the truth. It produces envy, quarrels, slander, and evil suspicions — all bitter fruits that poison the communal life of believers.
G3055.origine: The word comes from the Greek logos (word, reason, discourse) and machia (combat, quarrel). Its compound properly designates a "combat of words." The absence of harmony in these word disputes reflects the absence of charity: one prefers to win rather than to serve. It is the absolute contrast to the peace of Christ that the Apostle Paul urges to cultivate.
G3055.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 6:4, in the plural: "disputes about words." Paul addresses Timothy regarding the false teachers who have invaded the Church: they cling to "unprofitable questions" (vain, without spiritual benefit) and generate verbal quarrels. The Apostle establishes a clear link between these disputes of words, personal pride, and a degraded spiritual life. It is a warning addressed both to pastors and to all believers: to be careful not to let the love of discussion or dispute replace the thirst for truth and brotherly love.
G3055.portee: This word warns us against a subtle temptation: that of confusing the love of debate with the sincere pursuit of truth. A Christian can easily fall into "disputes about words" when he prefers to be right rather than to serve the unity of the Church or peace. Paul invites us to examine our motivations when we discuss spiritual matters: are we seeking to edify, or simply to shine? To clarify, or to dominate? This vigilance is essential to maintain the unity of the body of Christ and the purity of our testimony.

sens: A word, a unique utterance: a brief statement but full of meaning
A discourse, a set of words, a manner of speaking
A teaching, a doctrine, the instruction conveyed by a master
A matter, a question, a subject under discussion
The account, the obligation to give an account of one's actions
The Word of God, the divine revelation incarnated in Jesus Christ
G3056.detail: 1. The word 'word' primarily refers to a concrete utterance — not just a mere sound or an empty name, but a statement that expresses a thought, an idea, an intention. Matthew 5:37: "Let your word be 'yes, yes' or 'no, no'" perfectly illustrates this notion: a word that commits, that says something true. 2. 'Word' can also mean a discourse or a set of statements — the way one speaks, the style or effect of what is said. In 2 Corinthians 10:10, Paul is criticized for his "word" being contemptible: the speaker is judged by his manner of expression. 3. The word also refers to the teaching, the doctrine that is communicated. The "word of the Gospel" in Acts 15:7 is not a simple phrase, but the message of salvation, the Christian instruction received and believed. 4. 'Word' can signify a matter, a question under debate — a subject of dispute. Matthew 21:24: "By what authority are you doing these things?" poses a word, a question that demands an answer. 5. To give an account (in the expression "to render account"): the word carries the idea of a justification that must be presented. Hebrews 13:17 speaks of those who watch over your souls and who "will give an account." 6. In John 1:1 and 1:14, "the Word" (with a capital W) refers to Jesus Christ himself — not a mere statement, but the living revelation of God, "the Word made flesh."
G3056.origine: The Greek word logos comes from the verb legô (to say, to speak) and originally designates what is said, the utterance. It primarily translates the Hebrew dabar (word, thing, matter), a very rich word that carries both the idea of an utterance and that of a power that is fulfilled. In Greek philosophy, logos also means reason, rational principle — a less central meaning in the New Testament but which colors the prologue of John, where the Word is present with God and participates in creation. The notion is imbued with theological depth: the word becomes the instrument and manifestation of divine will.
G3056.emploi: The word logos is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (318 occurrences); Matthew, Mark, and Luke regularly use it to refer to the teaching of Jesus or his personal word. When Jesus speaks, it is said that he "utters words," that he teaches the "word of the Kingdom." In Paul and in the epistles, "the word of God" or "the word of the Lord" refers to the Gospel, the message to be proclaimed and believed. In John, particularly at the beginning (John 1:1-14), the word rises in dignity: the Word is the very actor of creation, and it is incarnated in Jesus Christ. The meaning varies according to the context: simple utterance, teaching, matter to debate, obligation of account rendering, or major revelation of divinity.
G3056.portee: For the Christian, "word" reminds us that faith comes from hearing (Romans 10:17) and that the Gospel is not an abstraction but a word received, retained, put into practice. Let our word be true and simple as Jesus teaches (Matthew 5:37): it is a call to honesty and transparency. The "Word of God" invites us to recognize that Jesus is not just a teacher who speaks, but the Word of God himself, in whom all that God is and what he accomplishes for our salvation is expressed.

sens: a spear, consisting of a metal tip fixed to the end of a shaft
the act of piercing with a spear
G3057.detail:
1. A spear is a weapon of war formed of a long wooden shaft topped with a sharpened metal point. It is the weapon of soldiers and warriors of antiquity. In the Gospel of John, it is with a spear that a Roman soldier pierces the side of the crucified Christ, thus fulfilling the very heart of his sacrifice (John 19:34).
2. The word also designates the action of striking or piercing with a spear. This final act in the Passion narrative reveals the reality of Christ's death: blood and water flow from his side, tangible signs that the Son of God truly suffered and shed his blood for us.
G3057.origine: The Greek word logchē comes from an ancient root designating a pointed weapon. It is a common term in the Greek language for a spear, found in historical and military texts. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew romach, which has the same meaning. The spear is one of humanity's oldest weapons, symbolizing both warrior power and, in the Christian context, the extreme violence inflicted on the Lord.
G3057.emploi: The word logchē appears only once in the New Testament as we have it, in John 19:34. In this verse, after Jesus' death on the cross, a Roman soldier thrusts his spear into the side of the Crucified. This act, although performed out of contempt or curiosity by the soldier, carries profound theological significance for John: it attests to the physical reality of Christ's death and his bloody sacrifice. The detail of blood and water flowing emphasizes the authentic humanity of the Savior and his complete self-giving.
G3057.portee: The spear that pierces the side of Christ reminds us that the Passion is not a theological abstraction, but a real historical event, where the Son of God bore suffering and death in his flesh. This ultimate wound becomes for the believer the sign of Christ's perfect love, who gives everything down to the last drop of his blood. It invites us to contemplate the intensity of the sacrifice and to respond with gratitude and dedication.

sens: To address someone with offensive, contemptuous, or insulting words
To insult someone with reproaches or accusations
To suffer insults, to be insulted
G3058.detail:
1. To injure is to say mean and hurtful words to someone in order to offend or belittle them. In John 9:28, the Pharisees insult the healed man by shouting harsh words at him; in Acts 23:4, Paul is accused of insulting the high priest. It is an attack with words, with the intention to cause harm.
2. An insult can take the form of a violent accusation or reproach. It is to belittle someone verbally, treating them as unworthy.
3. The verb is also used in the passive form to indicate that one suffers insults. In 1 Corinthians 4:12, Paul states that the apostles, when they are insulted, respond with a blessing; in 1 Peter 2:23, Jesus, insulted on the cross, does not return insult for insult. It is the experience of being despised in words and facing it with dignity.
G3058.origine: The Greek word comes from λοίδορος, which refers to coarse speech, an insult. The family of the word speaks of violent and mean language. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates the word קָלַל (to belittle, to curse) with this verb, expressing the idea of diminishing someone through words.
G3058.emploi: The verb injure appears four times in the New Testament, all instances provided. It describes situations where harsh words are exchanged: the Pharisees insult the healed blind man (John 9:28), Paul is accused of insulting the priest (Acts 23:4). But the word takes on a spiritual significance when it describes the suffering of the disciples or of Christ: Paul teaches that in the face of insults, one should bless (1 Corinthians 4:12), and this is the conduct of Christ himself during the passion (1 Peter 2:23). The context shows a progression: from the act of insulting to the example of one who, insulted, responds with good.
G3058.portee: This word invites the reader to confront two realities: on one hand, insults are a painful reality that disciples must face; on the other hand, the example of Christ and the teaching of Paul show that one can endure them without returning evil for evil. It is a call to imitate Jesus' reaction to insults: to maintain dignity, not to retaliate, and to entrust oneself to God who judges justly. This does not minimize the suffering but transforms it into an opportunity to manifest grace.

sens: Offensive, insulting, dishonoring word
Set of reproaches or malicious criticisms
Reason given to an opponent to criticize or attack us
G3059.detail:
1. An injury is a mean word that seeks to offend, humiliate, or shame someone. It is an insult directed at a person to strike at their honor. In 1 Peter 3:9, the term specifically refers to those hurtful words that people direct at one another and that a Christian should not return to one who strikes them.
2. An injury can also refer to a malicious reproach or accusation, a hostile discourse that seeks to discredit. It stands in opposition to blessing and words of grace.
3. More broadly, an injury is an opportunity given to an opponent (whether human or spiritual) to attack or criticize: in 1 Timothy 5:14, not giving an occasion for injury means not providing those who observe us with a valid reason to slander or condemn us.
G3059.origine: The Greek word λοιδορία comes from the verb λοιδορέω (to insult, to cover with curses), which expresses the action of launching outrageous words. This verb conveys the idea of a deliberate and aggressive verbal attack. In Hebrew, this word mainly translates רִיב (quarrel, dispute) and מְרִיבָה (quarrel, controversy), which express hostility and tension between people.
G3059.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, always to denote behavior to avoid. In 1 Timothy 5:14, Paul advises young women to manage their households well so as not to give a "pretext for injury" to adversaries (that is, not to leave them a reason to slander them). In 1 Peter 3:9, Peter calls Christians not to return "injury for injury," but rather to bless: it is about breaking the cycle of vengeance through words. In both contexts, injury represents the sin of speech that Christians must absolutely flee from.
G3059.portee: This word reminds Christians that our reputation and testimony also depend on our words and daily conduct. It teaches us that hurting someone with insults is contrary to the call to blessing that we have received. Refusing injury means choosing grace over vengeance, and creating around us a space of peace and respect.

sens: Who utters insults, hurtful words
Who behaves with verbal contempt towards others
Characterized by abusive speech and lack of respect
G3060.detail:
1. The word designates a person who hurls insults and coarse words at others. It is someone who hurts with their tongue, who does not hold back their offensive words. In 1 Corinthians 5:11, Paul classifies the "outrageous" alongside the immoral or drunkard: it is a serious defect that disqualifies the one affected from the communal life of the Church.
2. More broadly, it is an attitude of contempt expressed through words: treating someone with disdain, mocking them, humiliating them publicly or privately. In 1 Corinthians 6:10, Paul reminds that "the outrageous" will not inherit the kingdom of God, grouping this vice with theft, drunkenness, and other serious sins: it is an obstacle to eternal life.
3. The word can also describe a general character of verbal contempt, a habit of doing harm through words rather than actions.
G3060.origine: The Greek word λοίδορος comes from a root that evokes outrage and verbal insult. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew דִּין (din), which refers to quarrel or conflict (Proverbs 25:24 and 27:15 speak of a quarrelsome woman). The link is clear: the outrageous one is the one who creates discord through their tongue.
G3060.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's letters to the Corinthians. In 1 Corinthians 5:11, Paul lists the types of people with whom Christians should not maintain fraternal relations — the Church must correct or exclude the one who utters outrages. In 1 Corinthians 6:10, Paul poses the same question in another way: by reminding that such people will not inherit the kingdom, he places verbal insult on the same level as other forms of sin that exclude from eternal life. The context shows that Paul takes very seriously the harm caused by words.
G3060.portee: This word reminds Christians that words are powerful and that insults, mockery, and verbal contempt are serious sins — no less serious than drunkenness or theft. It calls for vigilance over our tongue: to become "outrageous" is to stray from the Gospel. It is also an exhortation to cultivate gentleness and respect in speech, as a fruit of the Spirit.

sens: Contagious and deadly disease that ravages a population
Figuratively, a person who is harmful to the community
G3061.detail:
1. The plague is an epidemic disease that spreads rapidly and kills many people. Jesus lists it among the great disasters of the end times, alongside earthquakes and famines (Luke 21:11: "There will be great earthquakes, and in various places, plagues and famines"). It is a natural scourge, terrifying and uncontrollable.
2. The word also applies to a person who causes harm to the community, who corrupts it from within like a disease. Paul refers to the leader of the Nazarenes as a "plague" (Acts 24:5: "We have found this man to be a plague, who stirs up dissension among all the Jews throughout the world"). The image is that of a poison or a moral infection that spreads and destroys harmony.
G3061.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to turn," "to deviate." Its primary image is that of something that deviates from good, that strays from the natural and healthy order, hence the idea of scourge or calamity. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates several Hebrew words denoting evil, destruction, or what is worthless, such as impiety or ruin.
G3061.emploi: The word λοιμός appears three times in the New Testament. Two occurrences describe the plague as a natural and eschatological disaster: Matthew 24:7 mentions it among the signs of the end of the world, and Luke 21:11 reiterates it in the same terms. A third occurrence (Acts 24:5) applies the word to a person: the accuser Tertullus calls Paul a "plague" to discredit him before the Roman governor Felix, accusing him of disturbing the peace. The meaning thus shifts from physical scourge to social scourge: a person who divides and harms.
G3061.portee: This word reminds us that true scourges are not only diseases or natural disasters: they are also people who sow division and discord in the Church and society. It invites discernment about who heals and who divides, who brings life and who brings corruption. For the Christian, it is a call to flee what destroys unity and to build what edifies.

sens: That which remains, that which subsists when the rest has disappeared
That which has not been mentioned or designated previously, in contrast to this one or those
The remaining people or things from a group
The time that comes, the future
In a broader sense: the others, the outsiders
G3062.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what remains, what subsists. In Luke 12:26, Jesus asks: "If then you cannot do even the least thing, why are you anxious about the rest?" — it is what remains after a part has been taken away.
2. It also designates what has not been named or distinguished before: "the others" in relation to "this one." In Matthew 22:6, "the other servants" are those not yet mentioned, distinct from the first.
3. Very often it is used in the plural to refer to people from a group who are excluded or who remain outside: in Acts 5:13, "none of the others dared to join" the apostles — referring to non-believers, those from outside.
4. By extension, "the rest of the time" or simply "afterwards," as in 1 Corinthians 7:29: "for the rest, let those who have wives" — it is a way of saying "besides" or "now." 
5. The word can also introduce an addition or a logical continuation: "furthermore, besides." In 1 Timothy 5:20, "so that the others may also experience fear" — it is so that the other witnesses may learn a lesson.
G3062.origine: The word comes from the verb λείπω ("to leave, abandon"), hence its fundamental meaning: "that which is left, that which remains." The root evokes the idea of what is left after subtraction. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament translates this word with terms like יָתַר ("to remain, to dwell") and שְׁאָר ("that which remains"), words that share this image of subsistence after a decrease. The word is thus naturally linked to the idea of incompletion: there is "the rest" because something is missing.
G3062.emploi: The word appears about 41 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in Revelation. It functions in three ways. First, in the plural "the others" to designate a distinct or excluded group: in Acts 5:13, the unbelievers who do not dare to join the believers; in Galatians 2:13, "the other Jews" who imitate Peter in his hypocrisy. Secondly, it is used in the neuter singular "the rest" or "for the rest" to mark a logical continuation or conclusion: in 1 Corinthians 7:29, "for the rest" introduces a new teaching. Finally, it can simply designate "that which remains" in the literal sense, as in Luke 12:26, where it concerns material concerns. Its usage varies: sometimes inclusive ("all the others"), sometimes exclusive ("the others" opposed to a privileged group), sometimes simply logical ("besides").
G3062.portee: This word invites the reader to discern who the "others" are in the Church and the world. It raises the question: am I on the side of those who remain outside, or on the side of the called? At the same time, it reminds us that God also cares for "all the others," whom we must not despise or neglect. Its use by Paul to introduce exhortations reminds us that faith is also a matter of "afterwards," of faithfulness in the continuation of life, not just an initial moment.

sens: That which remains, the remaining part of a whole
The other people, those who remain
Now, from this moment
Finally, after a long wait
Moreover, furthermore, to conclude
G3063.detail:
1. The primary meaning is "that which remains": the portion of a whole from which the rest has already been removed or consumed. For example, in Mark 4:19, the "other cares" are those that remain to occupy the heart beyond the primary concern.

2. It also designates "the other people," "those who remain." In Acts 2:37, Peter speaks to the crowd of Jews who remained, "the others," distinct from those who just believed.

3. When it takes the form of a neuter accusative and functions as a fixed phrase, it means "for the rest of the time," "henceforth," "from now on." In Matthew 26:45 and Mark 14:41, Jesus tells his disciples: "you are sleeping now" — from this moment, the end is approaching.

4. It can mean "finally," marking a conclusion after a long wait or a series of events. In Acts 27:20, in the midst of the storm, Paul says, "we finally lost all hope" — after days without sun or stars, despair sets in.

5. In introducing a conclusion or final point, it means "moreover," "furthermore," "to conclude." In 2 Corinthians 13:11 and Philippians 4:8, Paul uses it to launch his final exhortations: "Finally, brothers, rejoice."
G3063.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "leiô" which means "to leave" or "to abandon." The adjective "loipos" primarily depicts what remains when something has been taken away or set aside — hence "the rest," "the others." In Hebrew, it often translates "yathar" (to remain, to subsist) or "shear" (rest, residuum). This root of "to leave" explains how the word naturally shifts from spatial meaning (that which remains) to temporal meaning (that which remains to come, hence "henceforth").
G3063.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Greek New Testament. It has two main usages. First, the nominal usage: "the others," "the rest" (Matthew 22:6, Acts 2:37, Romans 1:13). Secondly, the adverbial usage, where the neuter form "to loipon" or "tou loipon" functions as a fixed phrase introducing a conclusion or a change of tone. When it means "henceforth," "now," it marks a temporal turning point (Matthew 26:45, Mark 14:41, 1 Corinthians 7:29). When it means "moreover," "finally," it serves as a rhetorical hinge to launch the final instructions of a letter (2 Corinthians 13:11, Philippians 4:8, 2 Thessalonians 3:1). The adverb "loipon" (transliteration provided) is this same form frozen in adverbial usage.
G3063.portee: This word helps the reader grasp the turning points in biblical discourse. When Paul writes "finally, brothers," he calls for a change of heart, a final exhortation before the end of his letter. When Jesus says "now," he marks the irruption of the Kingdom, the turning of the ages. Understanding this small word shows how biblical authors structure their thought and call for a new response, here and now.

sens: From now on, for the future
G3064.detail: 1. Paul uses this word to mean "from now on": he will no longer accept being troubled, for he bears the marks of Jesus on his body (Galatians 6:17). It is a turning point: what happened before is in the past; what matters is the future. 2. In Greek, the same word can also mean "for the rest" or "in the rest": it serves as a transition to move to a new subject, as when Paul writes "finally, be strong in the Lord" (Ephesians 6:10). Here, he closes one thought and opens another.
G3064.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb λείπω (to leave, to abandon). λοιπός primarily denotes what remains after something has been left or taken: "the rest." From there, it takes on the meaning of "what comes after," "what remains before us" — hence "from now on," "henceforth." In Hebrew, a similar range of meanings can be found with the word יָתַר (yathar), which means both "to remain" and "to exceed" or "to persist."
G3064.emploi: This word appears twice in the Segond in the given passages. In Galatians 6:17, Paul uses it to mark a clear break: "from now on, do not trouble me anymore." In Ephesians 6:10, it serves as a stylistic hinge: "finally" introduces a new exhortation. The context shows that λοιποῦ (in the neuter accusative singular) functions as a small adverbial phrase, fixed in a formula, rather than as an adjective attached to a noun.
G3064.portee: This word reminds us that the Christian faith is not just a matter of the past or present, but of orientation toward the future. When Paul says "from now on," he means that what he has experienced in Christ — his sufferings, his marks — redefines all his future. For us, "from now on" can mean: now that we know Christ, our life shifts, it changes course.

sens: companion and collaborator of the apostle Paul
physician by training
author of the Gospel and the Acts
G3065.detail: Luke is a companion of Paul mentioned three times in the Pauline epistles. In Colossians 4:14, Paul refers to him as "the beloved physician," indicating his medical profession and his affectionate status in the missionary team. In 2 Timothy 4:11, at a time when Paul feels isolated in Rome before his martyrdom, Luke remains his only support: "Only Luke is with me," showing his faithfulness in trial. In Philemon 1:24, he is listed among Paul's "fellow workers," alongside Mark, Aristarchus, and Demas, confirming his active role in the apostolic ministry. According to early church tradition, Luke is the author of the Gospel that bears his name and of the book of Acts, making him the principal historian of the early Christianity.
G3065.origine: The name Luke (Greek Loukas) is probably an abbreviation of the Latin name Lucius. It was a common name in the Greco-Roman world of that time. The Pauline context indicates that he was a man of pagan origin (unlike Mark and Aristarchus) who embraced the Christian faith and dedicated himself to Paul and the evangelistic mission.
G3065.emploi: Luke appears three times in the preserved Pauline epistles: in Colossians 4:14, where Paul refers to him as the beloved physician sending greetings to the church in Colossae; in 2 Timothy 4:11, in Paul's final thoughts where he sees him as his last faithful support; and in Philemon 1:24, where he is presented as a Christian worker alongside other collaborators of Paul. These three occurrences show him as a figure of trust and stability in the apostolic ministry. Later Christian tradition identifies him as the author of the third Gospel and of Acts, making him a central figure in the New Testament.
G3065.portee: Luke's faithfulness to Paul in difficult times (especially in 2 Timothy 4:11) offers a model of persistent commitment to Christ and to those who serve his cause. His identity as a physician dedicated to ministry shows that God values and uses professional talents for the advancement of the Gospel. For the modern reader, Luke reminds us of the importance of discreet and faithful collaborators in missionary work and the Church.

sens: Man from Cyrene, prophet and teacher in Antioch
Roman Christian, relative of Paul, who greets him in his letter to the Romans
G3066.detail:
1. Lucius of Cyrene is mentioned in Acts 13:1 as one of the prophets and teachers of the Church in Antioch, alongside Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Manaen, and Saul. He comes from North Africa (Cyrene is in Libya) and exercises a prophetic ministry in the first Christian community.
2. Another Lucius, this one Roman, is greeted by the apostle Paul in Romans 16:21; Paul calls him his relative, indicating a familial bond or particular closeness. He accompanies Paul in sending the letter to the Romans.
G3066.origine: Lucius is a common Latin name in the Roman Empire, derived from the Latin root lux (light). It is a name that the Bible receives from the Greco-Roman world without translation. The name underscores the Roman and Western roots of early Christianity, beyond Jerusalem and the Semitic world.
G3066.emploi: Lucius appears twice in the New Testament. The first, in Acts 13:1, is a prophet and teacher from Antioch, making him one of the prominent figures of the second Christian generation at the time of the departure of the first Pauline mission. The second, in Romans 16:21, is presented as related to Paul and part of the circle of the apostle's fellow workers. It is unclear whether this is the same person or two different individuals: tradition cannot affirm it.
G3066.portee: These two mentions illustrate the expansion of Christianity beyond Judea and the involvement of converted pagan Christians, from Cyrene or Rome, in the apostolic ministry. The name Lucius reminds the reader that the Gospel spread rapidly in the Greco-Roman world, integrating men of various origins into the mission of the Church.

sens: The act of washing, purifying oneself with water
A bath or immersion in water
A rite of purification or religious initiation
G3067.detail:
1. The word first describes the concrete act of washing or cleansing something: to plunge into water for cleaning. It conveys the idea of a physical ablution, a material act of purification by water.
2. It denotes a bath or immersion, meaning a complete passage of the body or object into the water. The water itself is the means of transformation: in Ephesians 5:26, Paul speaks of the "water baptism" that purifies the Church.
3. In the biblical religious context, the word takes on the meaning of a rite of initiation or consecration: a solemn act that marks a break and a spiritual renewal. In Titus 3:5, the "baptism of regeneration" signifies not just a simple material washing, but an inner transformation brought about by the work of the Holy Spirit.
G3067.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "to wash" (λούω, louô). It often translates the Hebrew רַחְצָה (rahtsah), which means "washing" or "ablution," in the Greek Old Testament. At the time of the New Testament, baptism was a well-known religious gesture: John immersed people in the waters of the Jordan as a sign of repentance and purification.
G3067.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Ephesians 5:26, Paul uses the image of "water baptism" to show how Christ purifies the Church through his word: it is a purification that is both physical (the water) and spiritual (the word). In Titus 3:5, Paul speaks of the "baptism of regeneration," meaning what is born anew in us, not by our efforts but "by the renewal of the Holy Spirit." In both cases, baptism is a transformative act: it purifies and renews.
G3067.portee: This word reminds Christians that baptism, whether viewed as an external rite or an internal experience, is an act of purification and renewal. It is not merely a personal decision, but a transformation brought about by the word of God and by the Spirit. For the baptized, it means being separated from sin and consecrated to the Lord.

sens: to bathe, to wash the entire body
to clean a wound or injury
to be washed (passive or reflexive)
to purify, to clean in a figurative sense
G3068.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to wash the entire body or to immerse in water: when washing a dead person, one bathes them completely (Acts 9:37), or when washing someone's wounds, one carefully cleans their body (Acts 16:33).
2. The word also denotes a complete cleansing of the body with water, as when it is said that hearts are washed from an evil conscience and the body washed with pure water (Hebrews 10:22).
3. Used in the passive or reflexive sense, it evokes the action of washing oneself or being washed (John 13:10: "He who is washed needs only to wash his feet").
4. In a figurative sense, it expresses spiritual purification: to wash someone in the blood of Christ means to cleanse them from their sins (Revelation 1:5, although this passage differs in some versions).
G3068.origine: The Greek verb λούω comes from an ancient root meaning to dip or immerse. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates this word as רָחַץ (rachatz), which refers to both daily washing and ritual ablutions mandated by the Law. The word belongs to a rich semantic field: νίπτω (nipô) is used for washing hands, feet, and face; πλύνω (plunô) for washing clothes or objects. λούω is the broadest, covering bathing or immersing the entire body.
G3068.emploi: The verb λούω appears 5 times in the provided New Testament. It first refers to the care of bodies: washing a corpse (Acts 9:37) or the wounds of a prisoner (Acts 16:33). It also appears in the passive or reflexive to describe the state of purity after washing (John 13:10, Hebrews 10:22). A proverbial occurrence in 2 Peter 2:22 plays on the image of a washed pig returning to wallow in the mud, stigmatizing one who returns to their former sins. The context is often that of purification, whether physical or spiritual.
G3068.portee: This word helps the Christian understand that baptism and the cleansing of the heart by faith are compared to the washing of the body. To be washed is to be completely purified, to become new. It also sheds light on why Jesus washes the feet of his disciples: this act reminds us that continual spiritual purification is necessary, and that it comes through humility and service.

sens: City in Palestine located between Jerusalem and the Mediterranean coast
G3069.detail: 1. Lydda is a Palestinian city from the apostolic era, located near Joppa (modern Jaffa) on the coastal road. It is where the apostle Peter goes to visit the local churches (Acts 9:32), and where he performs a miracle by healing a paralyzed man named Aeneas, which leads to the conversion of many inhabitants of Lydda and the region of Sharon (Acts 9:35). The city is mentioned as a strategic geographical landmark: the disciples from Joppa send for Peter in Lydda, which is not far away (Acts 9:38).
G3069.origine: Lydda transcribes the Hebrew name לֹד (Lod). It is an ancient city of Canaan mentioned in the Old Testament (1 Chronicles 8:12). The Greek name Λύδδα simply reflects the Hebrew pronunciation adapted to the Greek phonetic system. The city existed long before the New Testament era and retained its commercial and administrative importance under Roman rule.
G3069.emploi: Lydda appears three times in Acts (9:32, 35, 38), exclusively in the account of Peter's visit. Luke mentions it as an important city in Judea, sufficiently populated and organized to host a community of believers. The context shows that it was a center of early Christian life in Palestine, located on the routes of trade and apostolic travels. The healing of Aeneas there provokes a massive spiritual turnaround.

sens: Woman from Thyatira converted to the Gospel by the apostle Paul
Seller of purple who welcomed Paul and Silas into her home
G3070.detail:
1. Lydia is a woman from the city of Thyatira in Asia Minor. She is described as a seller of purple, meaning a wealthy merchant who sold fabric dyed in purple, a precious and costly dye. Her profession indicates that she enjoyed a certain respectability and resources (Acts 16:14).
2. Lydia is best known as the first convert to the Christian faith on the European continent. During Paul's second missionary journey, she listens to the message of the Gospel in Philippi, where she was praying by the river with other women. The apostle recounts that the Lord opened her heart to receive Paul's message (Acts 16:14).
3. After her conversion, she generously offered hospitality to Paul and his companion Silas. She welcomed them into her home, thus becoming a support base for the apostolic ministry. When Paul was released from prison in Philippi, he first went to her house to encourage the brothers, which shows the importance of her role in the nascent Christian community (Acts 16:40).
G3070.origine: The name Lydia is derived from ancient Greek, likely related to the historical region of Lydia in Asia Minor, known for its commerce and wealth. This is not a certain etymology, but the name evokes the geographical origins of this woman or her area of commercial activity.
G3070.emploi: Lydia appears twice in Acts, exclusively in the account of Paul's second missionary journey in Philippi (Acts 16:14, 40). In the first passage, she is introduced as a God-fearing woman, a category of people who worshiped the God of Israel without being formally converted to Judaism. Paul speaks to her, and she becomes the first person converted to the Christian faith in Europe. In the second passage, her home serves as a refuge and gathering place for young Christians. These two occurrences portray her as a key figure in the establishment of the Church in Macedonia.
G3070.portee: Lydia embodies the role of women in the expansion of the Gospel in the early days of the Church. Her example shows that conversion is not a private event: it immediately compels her to open her home, her resources, and her life to the Christian community. Her hospitality becomes a ministry, reminding believers that generosity and welcome are natural fruits of the Gospel. She also teaches us that receptivity to the message of Jesus truly transforms a person, as it was the Lord himself who opened her heart.

sens: historical region of Asia Minor
G3071.detail: Lycaonia is a geographical region located in what corresponds to modern central Turkey. It was a province of the ancient world, with its own cities and population.
G3071.origine: The word is the Greek name for a region in Asia Minor. Its exact etymology remains uncertain, but it designated a well-known area in antiquity, particularly under Roman rule.
