G3071.emploi: Lycaonia is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Acts 14:6. Paul and Barnabas take refuge there after facing hostility in Iconium. Lystra and Derbe, the two main cities named in the same verse, were located in Lycaonia. It is in Lystra that Paul heals a crippled man (Acts 14:8-10), an event that will provoke an attempt to deify him.

sens: Word, speech spoken in the language of Lycaonia
G3072.detail: 1. The Lycaonian language is the dialect or language spoken by the inhabitants of Lycaonia, a region of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). In Lystra, a city in Lycaonia, the crowd that sees Paul heal a cripple cries out in their own local language to say that the gods have come to visit men (Acts 14:11). It was the speech of the ordinary people of that area, different from the Greek used by educated individuals.
G3072.origine: The word comes from Lycaonia, the name of the ancient region in Asia Minor. The adverb in -στί marks the language or dialect in which one speaks. Lycaonia was a province in the heart of Asia Minor, with its inhabitants and their own way of speaking, distinct from the classical Greek widespread in the empire.
G3072.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 14:11. Paul is in Lystra, in Lycaonia, when he heals a lame man. The inhabitants, seeing this miracle, cry out in their own language to interpret the event as the arrival of the gods. This unique moment shows that Paul and Barnabas needed an interpreter or were listening to the spontaneous reaction of the people in their vernacular, proving that the good news must reach everyone in their own language.
G3072.portee: This word reminds us that the Gospel is addressed to all peoples in their own language and culture, without disdain for local idioms. The Lycaonian crowd, even if they mix the event with their beliefs, hears the message in their own voice—a lesson on universality and respect for the diversity of languages in Christian proclamation.

sens: region of ancient Asia Minor
G3073.detail: Lycia is a coastal region in the southwest of Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey). It is located on the Mediterranean, between Cilicia and Pamphylia. Paul passes through it on his journey to Rome as a prisoner: the ship that transports him crosses the adjacent seas and arrives at Myra, its main city. This geographical mention precisely situates the stage of Paul's missionary journey.
G3073.origine: The Greek name Λυκία (Lukia) designates this ancient historical region of Asia Minor. Myra, mentioned in the biblical verse as a city of Lycia, was an important port in this region.
G3073.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 27:5. Paul, a prisoner on a Roman ship en route to Rome, passes through this region. The mention of Lycia serves to document the precise geographical itinerary of the journey, showing how the message of Christ extends to the ends of the known world of the Romans.

sens: wild carnivorous animal that hunts sheep
dangerous and cruel person who attacks the weak
false prophet or bad shepherd disguised as a friend
G3074.detail:
1. The wolf is a predatory animal that attacks flocks of sheep: it is the natural enemy of the shepherd. In John 10:12, the wolf "snatches and scatters" the sheep when the shepherd is not vigilant.

2. By extension, a wolf refers to a cruel, exploitative person who attacks the innocent and the weak. In Acts 20:29, Paul warns that "savage wolves" will come in among Christians to devastate them.

3. Figuratively, the wolf represents the false prophet or the bad shepherd: someone who appears harmless on the surface but hides devastating intentions. In Matthew 7:15, false prophets "come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves." The image warns: beware of deceptive appearances.
G3074.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and simply designates the wolf, this well-known animal in the Mediterranean. In the Hebrew Old Testament, the term used is זְאֵב (zeév) for the same animal. The Bible uses the image of the wolf because it was familiar to its readers: the wolf was a real danger for shepherds in the Middle East, and its predatory nature made it a powerful symbol of threat and deception.
G3074.emploi: The word "wolf" appears 5 times in the Gospels and Acts, always with a strong symbolic charge. In Matthew 10:16 and Luke 10:3, Jesus sends his disciples "as sheep among wolves," emphasizing that they will be vulnerable and threatened. In Matthew 7:15, the image serves to describe false prophets who resemble authentic believers but actually want to devastate the Church. In John 10:12, the wolf illustrates the danger for those who do not have a true shepherd. In Acts 20:29, Paul transfers the image to bad teachers who come in after him. Each time, the word evokes deception, cruelty, and hidden danger.
G3074.portee: This image of the wolf reminds Christians that the threat does not always come from clearly identified outsiders, but often from those who pretend to be friends or guides. It invites spiritual vigilance without paranoia: to discern the teachings and motives of those who approach us, especially leaders. It also teaches that following Jesus may expose the believer to hostility, but this vulnerability is not a weakness—it is the lot of those who belong to Him.

sens: to treat brutally, to mistreat
to destroy, to devastate
to corrupt, to defile
G3075.detail:
1. To ravage primarily means to treat someone or something with violence and cruelty, to severely mistreat. This is what Saul did in persecuting the Church: he entered houses to drag off men and women and throw them into prison (Acts 8:3), thus destroying Christian communities from within.
2. The word also evokes the action of destroying, completely devastating, as one ravages a country by plundering it. It is a violence that leaves ruins.
3. By extension, to ravage can mean to corrupt or defile, to morally or spiritually damage what was intact. This is why the word is used in the Old Testament to describe moral corruption or dishonor.
G3075.origine: The word comes from the root λύμη which denotes outrage, insult, shame. It is a verb formed to express the idea of bringing shame to someone, treating them ignominiously. In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew verb שָׁחַת ("to destroy, to corrupt"), showing that to ravage is both an external violence and an internal corruption. The word belongs to a family of expressions that describe destruction and humiliation.
G3075.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:3, in the dramatic context of the persecution of the early Christians. Saul (who will become the apostle Paul) "ravaged" the Church, meaning he was systematically bent on destroying it by imprisoning believers. This verb emphasizes the intensity and savagery of this persecution: it was not mere opposition, but a deliberate intent to do harm and destroy. In the Old Testament, the word translates Hebrew verbs that express total corruption or destruction, showing that the central idea is one of violence that annihilates or profanes.
G3075.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of the reality of the persecution that the early disciples endured and the intensity of Paul's conversion. Saul ravaged the Church until the moment he encountered the risen Christ on the road to Damascus. It is a call not to forget the price paid by those who confessed their faith, and to recognize that violence against the Church has never extinguished the Christian witness.

sens: To cause pain or sorrow to someone
To be afflicted, to feel sadness
To experience a moral pain that overwhelms the soul
G3076.detail:
1. To grieve someone is to cause them deep pain, a distress of the heart. Herod was grieved when John the Baptist asked him to renounce his wife (Matthew 14:9): the king felt the conflict between his conscience and his desires. It is a sadness caused by a word, a situation, a refusal, that penetrates the soul.
2. To be grieved is to experience this sadness, to feel it deep within oneself. The rich young man went away sad when Jesus told him to sell everything (Matthew 19:22): he was seized by sorrow and affliction. Peter was also grieved when Jesus asked him for the third time about love (John 21:17): the renewed reproach wounded him.
3. This sadness can be an affliction that oppresses the heart, especially in the face of death or separation. Paul wrote to the Corinthians with a heavy heart of affliction and shedding tears (2 Corinthians 2:4): his letter was not a threat, but the expression of his love for them, even if it had to grieve them.
G3076.origine: The word comes from the root λύπη (lypê), meaning pain, moral suffering. It is the verb that expresses the action of causing or feeling this pain. The root is ancient and initially describes physical pain, then the suffering of the heart. In Hebrew, it is often translated from חָרָה (charah), which means to burn with anger or grief.
G3076.emploi: The verb λυπέω appears 21 times in the New Testament. Paul frequently uses it to speak of correction in the Churches (2 Corinthians 2:2, 2:4, 2:5, 7:8, 7:9, 7:11): the severe letter he wrote first grieved the Corinthians, but this 'godly sorrow' led them to repentance. The Gospels encounter it mainly in accounts of refusal or suffering: the rich young man, the disciples learning of the Passion (Matthew 17:23), Herod facing John the Baptist. John reports Jesus' triple question to Peter (John 21:17), where the renewal of the challenge grieves the disciple. An important nuance: Paul distinguishes between 'godly sorrow,' which leads to repentance, and worldly sorrow, which leads to death (2 Corinthians 7:10). The apostle also warns not to grieve the Holy Spirit (Ephesians 4:30): our hurtful words, our bitterness grieve God's gift within us.
G3076.portee: This word reminds us that as Christians, we must weigh the weight of our words and actions: we have the power to grieve or to comfort those around us. But it also teaches that sadness, when it comes from God, can be good: it leads us to repentance and change. Finally, respecting the Holy Spirit means being careful not to contest God's presence within us through our harsh words or our rebellion.

sens: Pain or sorrow of the soul, feeling of deep affliction
State of dejection and sorrow that overwhelms the heart
Affliction caused by the lack or loss of what one loved
Sadness that arises from the consciousness of sin and produces repentance
Feeling opposed to joy and gladness
G3077.detail:
1. Sadness is primarily the inner pain, the affliction of the heart that overwhelms the soul. Jesus' disciples experience this sadness when he announces his departure: they are seized with sorrow at the thought of his absence (John 16:6, 20). It is the weight of a heart that collapses.

2. This sadness can become excessive and dangerous for the one who bears it. Paul encourages the Corinthians to comfort the one who has sinned, lest his sadness completely overwhelm him and lead him to despair (2 Corinthians 2:7).

3. Sadness can arise from the awareness of our sins or from indignation at evil. Paul confesses his deep sadness when thinking of those who are lost: 'I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart' (Romans 9:2).

4. Not all types of sadness are of equal value. There is a 'godly sorrow' — one that leads to recognizing evil and changing — and a 'worldly sorrow' — one that leads to despair and death (2 Corinthians 7:10).

5. Sadness is the direct opposite of joy. Jesus promises that the sadness of the disciples will turn into unending joy when they see him again (John 16:20, 22).
G3077.origine: The word λύπη (lupē) literally means 'pain' or 'sorrow.' In Greek, it primarily denotes moral suffering, the pain of the soul rather than physical pain. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew עֶצֶב (etsev), which also evokes pain, sorrow, and even the fatigue of work. The family of the word includes the verb λυπέω (lupéô), 'to grieve' or 'to sadden.' This root always expresses the idea of weight, of a burden that overwhelms.
G3077.emploi: The word appears 14 times in the New Testament, especially in Paul and John. John uses it in Jesus' farewell speeches, where he describes the sadness of the disciples at his imminent departure, but also the transformation of this sadness into joy (John 16:6, 20, 22). Paul, as a pastoral apostle, uses it to speak of the necessity to comfort those who are burdened (2 Corinthians 2:1, 7) and to distinguish good sadness — the one that leads to repentance — from bad sadness — the one that leads to death (2 Corinthians 7:10). It should also be noted that Paul advises to give 'without sadness,' meaning generously and with a good heart (2 Corinthians 9:7). The word also appears in passages speaking of trial and divine discipline (Hebrews 12:11).
G3077.portee: Sadness is presented in Scripture not as a sin, but as an inevitable reality of fallen human existence. What matters is that the believer does not become trapped in it: he must distinguish the sadness that comes from remorse over sin — which leads to repentance and salvation — from that which comes from pride or rebellion — which leads to death. Christ promises that the temporal sadness of the disciple will be transformed into eternal joy. This hope changes everything: it allows one to endure present pain knowing that it will not last.

sens: Tetrarch who governed Abilene at the time of Jesus
G3078.detail: Lysanias is a tetrarch (governor of a quarter of a territory) mentioned only once in the Gospel. He rules over Abilene, a region in northern Palestine, at the time when John the Baptist begins his ministry (Luke 3:1). Luke cites him alongside other political leaders of the time — Pontius Pilate, Herod, and Philip — to establish the exact historical context of John's ministry.
G3078.origine: The name Lysanias is Greek. It designates a king or prince of the region of Abilene, which corresponds to an area of present-day Lebanon. This name appears rarely in ancient sources: only Luke preserves it.
G3078.emploi: Lysanias appears only once in the Bible (Luke 3:1). Luke introduces him to precisely date the beginning of John the Baptist's preaching: he lists the civil and religious rulers of Palestine and the surrounding regions at that time, which demonstrates the historical accuracy of the Gospel account.

sens: Roman military officer, tribune of the Jerusalem garrison
the one who rescues Paul from the hands of the angry crowd
G3079.detail: Lysias is a Roman tribune, commander of the Antonia fortress stationed in Jerusalem. When the Jewish crowd rises against Paul in the Temple, it is Lysias who intervenes and frees him from the violence of his attackers (Acts 24:7). He then writes an official report to Governor Felix to present the case (Acts 23:26), and Felix requests that Lysias come to testify before rendering his judgment (Acts 24:22).
G3079.origine: Lysias is a common Greek name, borne by several historical figures from Greco-Roman antiquity. In this case, he is a Roman of Greek or Hellenized origin, as indicated by his full designation: Claudius Lysias (Claude Lysias in Latin). The prefix 'Claudius' shows that he belongs to the Roman imperial family of the Claudians.
G3079.emploi: Lysias appears three times in Acts, exclusively in the account of Paul's arrest and trial in Jerusalem (chapters 23-24). He is first named as the tribune who frees Paul from the hostile crowd (Acts 24:7), then as the author of an official letter to Governor Felix (Acts 23:26), and finally as the witness that Felix awaits to instruct the trial (Acts 24:22). His role illustrates Roman authority which, by protecting Paul, allows the Gospel to advance even in the face of opposition from Jewish authorities.
G3079.portee: The figure of Lysias shows how God uses civil authorities, even pagan ones, to protect His servants. The tribune is not a believer, but his providential intervention saves Paul from death and allows him to appear before the governor. It is a reminder that divine Providence acts through various means to accomplish its purposes.

sens: The state of being united in marriage
The conjugal bond that ties two spouses to each other
G3080.detail:
1. The word refers to the marriage bond, that is, the marital union itself in what constitutes it as a bond. In 1 Corinthians 7:27, Paul speaks of one who is 'bound to a woman': this bond is precisely the marriage that unites man and woman, and he urges not to 'break' it.
2. The conjugal bond is presented as something that ties, that attaches one person to another — a relationship of mutual dependence. This is why the passage speaks of seeking to 'break' this bond: the image is that of a chain, an attachment that can be undone.
G3080.origine: The word comes from the verb 'luo' which means 'to unbind, detach, break'. Conversely, 'lusis' thus designates what is bound, tied — hence the meaning of bond or union. In Ecclesiastes 8:1 (in the Greek Old Testament), the same word translates the Hebrew 'pesher' (explanation, solution). The common image is that of something tied that needs to be undone or elucidated.
G3080.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 7:27. Paul uses it when speaking of marital status: one who is bound to a woman should not seek to break this bond, while one who is not bound should not seek a woman. The context of this passage (1 Corinthians 7) deals with questions of marriage and single life in light of impending tribulations. The word 'bond' emphasizes that marriage is a union that ties the two spouses together.
G3080.portee: This passage helps the Christian understand marriage as a real and serious bond — not merely a social convention, but a true attachment between two people. It invites consideration of marital commitment with seriousness and not to dissolve it lightly. For the married person, it is a reminder that marriage is not an inert thing, but a living relationship that binds.

sens: To be profitable or beneficial for someone
To suit, to be better or more useful in a given situation
G3081.detail:
1. The word expresses what is useful, what truly benefits someone. It is the idea of a real advantage, of concrete utility. In Luke 17:2, Jesus says that it would be 'better' (more advantageous) for one who causes offense to the little ones to receive a millstone around his neck rather than face divine judgment — in other words, immediate physical destruction would be less terrible than eternal condemnation.
2. By extension, the word designates what is best in a comparison between two options: among several possibilities, it is the one that produces the greatest good or avoids the greatest harm. The context in Luke 17:2 plays on this comparison: two terrible fates are weighed against each other, and Jesus affirms which would be less harmful.
G3081.origine: The Greek word comes from two elements: 'lysis' (λύσις, dissolution, end) and 'telos' (τέλος, objective, result). The basic idea is 'one who settles accounts', that is, who produces a useful or profitable result. This root evokes the image of reaching a goal, achieving something beneficial. The word belongs to the family of 'lyo' (λύω, to unbind, dissolve) and 'teleos' (τέλειος, perfect, complete).
G3081.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 17:2. Jesus uses it in a solemn warning against one who causes offense to children or the little ones in faith. The verb is used in the impersonal form ('it would be advantageous'), followed by a comparison introduced by 'if... or': two punishments are weighed against each other to show which would truly be preferable. It is strong rhetorical language, where the expression of relative advantage serves to underscore the extreme gravity of divine judgment on scandal.
G3081.portee: This verse invites the believer to take seriously the protection of the weakest in faith. Jesus employs a shocking gradation — physical death would be 'more advantageous' than eternal judgment — to engrave in consciences that causing harm to the little ones is a sin of exceptional gravity. The word 'advantageous' forces us to reflect: what is truly good for me, truly useful for my soul? It is an invitation to orient one's life toward what truly benefits, that is, justice toward the weak and faithfulness to God.

sens: City of Lycaonia in Asia Minor
Important center of Pauline evangelization
G3082.detail:
1. Lystra is a city located in Lycaonia, a region in southern Asia Minor (present-day Turkey). Paul and Barnabas take refuge there after escaping from persecutors in Iconium, and it is there that the spectacular miracle of healing a man who was lame from birth occurs, leading the crowd to take Paul for a god (Acts 14:8-11).
2. The city becomes a hub of disciples: Paul returns there during his second missionary journey (Acts 14:21), discovers Timothy, a young man well spoken of among the local brothers, who will become his valuable collaborator (Acts 16:1-2). Lystra thus symbolizes for Paul a place of both suffering (the persecutions he endured there) and spiritual victory, as the Lord always delivered him from it (2 Timothy 3:11).
G3082.origine: The Greek name Lystra designates this ancient city of Lycaonia. Its actual history remains poorly documented outside the accounts in Acts, making it a place known primarily through the missionary activity of Paul and his companions.
G3082.emploi: Lystra appears six times in the New Testament, exclusively in the accounts of Paul in Acts and in his letter to Timothy. The three occurrences in chapter 14 of Acts describe Paul's and Barnabas's first visit: their arrival (14:6), the miracle of the healed lame man (14:8), and their return after evangelizing (14:21). The two occurrences in chapter 16 situate the second visit, where Paul meets and takes Timothy with him, whom the brothers from Lystra warmly recommend (16:1-2). Finally, Paul reminds Timothy of the trials he endured in Lystra, among other cities, to encourage him in perseverance (2 Timothy 3:11). Lystra is thus the birthplace of Timothy's ministry and a testimony to God's faithfulness to Paul.
G3082.portee: Lystra reminds Christians that faith often arises in small towns and far from major centers, where ordinary men and women become faithful disciples and useful servants of the Gospel. It is also a lesson in courage: despite the persecutions suffered in Lystra, Paul never gave up, and God's grace constantly supported him. Finally, Lystra is the place where Timothy's calling germinated, showing how the Gospel transforms a community and produces workers for the Kingdom.

sens: The price paid to free a captive or enslaved person
What redeems or delivers someone from a situation of slavery or debt
The sacrifice offered as compensation or for atonement
The life given in exchange for the salvation of others
G3083.detail:
1. A ransom is primarily the price paid to recover someone who has been captured, sold, or imprisoned — for example, to buy the freedom of a slave or to repay a debt that kept them in servitude. It is a commercial act: money or goods are exchanged for the liberation of a person.

2. In a figurative sense, it is what delivers someone from an unfortunate situation or slavery: what "redeems" their situation. Jesus uses this word to speak of his own death — his life is the ransom that frees others from their sins and judgment (Matthew 20:28 and Mark 10:45).

3. The word also suggests a sacrifice or compensation: something is offered in place of someone else, to spare them from the misfortune that threatened them. This is why the Church Fathers applied it to the death of Christ as payment for salvation.
G3083.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "luo" which means "to loose," "to untie." A ransom is therefore what looses or liberates someone. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates several Hebrew words: "pidyon" (the price of redemption), "geula" (redemption), "kofer" (atonement or the price of redemption). This family of words revolves around the idea of an act of liberation through payment or exchange.
G3083.emploi: The word "ransom" appears only twice in the New Testament, in two identical parallel passages: Matthew 20:28 and Mark 10:45. In these two verses, Jesus explains that the Son of Man came "to give his life as a ransom for many." This is the only time the New Testament directly applies this term to the death of Christ. The expression "ransom for many" means that Jesus' death frees a large number of people. The term emphasizes that it is not an accidental death, but a voluntary sacrifice offered for the salvation of others — a life given in exchange for the liberation of others.
G3083.portee: This word reveals the heart of the Gospel: Jesus does not die for himself, but for us. His life is the act of liberation that pulls us from sin and judgment. The term "ransom" shows that there is a real price for our salvation and that Jesus paid it with his own life. For a Christian, it is the assurance that their slavery to sin has an end — they have been redeemed. This should nourish gratitude and transform the way of living.

sens: To free someone by paying a ransom
To pay the price for someone's freedom
To deliver from slavery or captivity
In a spiritual sense: to save through sacrifice, to free from sin
G3084.detail:
1. The word first evokes the concrete image of a ransom paid to obtain the release of a prisoner or a slave. In 1 Peter 1:18, Paul explains that we have been "redeemed" not with gold or silver, but with the sacrifice of Christ — the idea of paying a price to obtain freedom.
2. This liberation is obtained by satisfying a debt or requirement. The one who pays the ransom settles what was owed, so that the captive may be free.
3. In a broader sense, the word means "to deliver" or "to liberate." Luke 24:21 shows this: the disciples hoped that Jesus would "deliver" Israel — not just redeeming them from financial captivity, but freeing them from Roman domination.
4. The New Testament applies this image to spiritual salvation. Titus 2:14 states that Jesus "gave himself for us, to redeem us from all iniquity" — meaning that he paid with his own sacrifice the price of our liberation from sin.
G3084.origine: The word comes from λύτρον (lutron), the ransom or price of redemption. The root expresses the idea of "to loose" or "to release" in exchange for payment. In Hebrew, the root גָּאַל (gaal, "to redeem") or פָּדָה (padah, "to ransom") expressed the same notion in the Old Testament — that of a relative or redeemer who pays the price to reclaim a family member sold into slavery.
G3084.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament. Luke 24:21 uses it in a political sense: the disciples hoped that Jesus would deliver Israel from Roman rule. But it is especially in the epistles that the term reveals its spiritual significance. In Titus 2:14, Paul states that Christ "gave himself for us," establishing an explicit link between sacrifice and the redemption of our sins. In 1 Peter 1:18, Peter emphasizes that this redemption did not cost earthly goods, but "the precious blood of Christ." The context always shows that to redeem is to pay a price to free someone from a condition of servitude or guilt.
G3084.portee: This word transforms our understanding of salvation. Jesus did not simply forgive our sins: he paid a price, like a parent who redeems a child sold into slavery. This biblical image of ransom and redemption reminds us that our freedom in Christ has infinite value — that of the blood of the Son of God. It frees us from guilt, from the slavery of sin, and restores our lost dignity.

sens: Purchase or ransom to free someone from slavery or captivity
Liberation, deliverance of a people or a person from an unfortunate condition
The salvific and sacrificial work of Christ that frees us from sin and death
G3085.detail:
1. The word first evokes the concrete image of redemption: paying a ransom to rescue someone from slavery or captivity. It is an exchange: a price is given to obtain the freedom of a person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this price was often in money (Numbers 18:16 speaks of the redemption price of firstborns).

2. The word then broadens to designate the liberation of an entire people from a difficult or oppressive condition. When Zechariah says, "God has visited and redeemed his people" (Luke 1:68), he speaks of the deliverance of all of Israel. It is God's action coming to save his people from servitude or misfortune.

3. In the New Testament, the word takes on its highest meaning: the work of salvation accomplished by Christ. In Hebrews 9:12, the apostle explains that Christ, through the sacrifice of his own blood shed once for all, has obtained eternal redemption. It is the infinite price paid to free us from sin and death; it is the definitive and universal redemption offered to all who believe.
G3085.origine: The word λύτρωσις (lutrôsis) comes from the verb λυτρόω (lutroô), which means "to redeem" or "to liberate by ransom." The root evokes the idea of paying a price to obtain freedom. In Hebrew, this concept is rendered by several words depending on the context: גְּאֻלָּה (gueoulah, "redemption"), פָּדָה (padah, "to redeem"), and פִּדְיוֹם (pidyom, "ransom"). All these Hebrew words carry the image of a divine intervention to liberate his people.
G3085.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. Twice in Luke, in the context of the birth of Jesus: Zechariah praises God who "has redeemed his people" (Luke 1:68), and Simeon and Anna speak of those who "were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem" (Luke 2:38) — these passages look to the messianic promise and the awaited liberation of Israel. Once in Hebrews 9:12, where the apostle affirms that Christ has "obtained eternal redemption" through his unique and perfect sacrifice — here the word reaches its full and eternal meaning: the redemption accomplished definitively by the Messiah for all believers.
G3085.portee: Redemption is not a distant abstraction: it is the expression of the heart of the Gospel. God does not leave us captive to sin; he pays the supreme price — the blood of Christ — to buy us and set us free. This redemption is both personal (it changes my life) and universal (it is offered to all). For the Christian, understanding what redemption is means grasping that their freedom has a price, that their deliverance comes from God alone, and that this freedom won by Christ is definitive and eternal.

sens: one who delivers someone from servitude, danger, or oppression
one who saves, who redeems
G3086.detail:
1. A liberator is someone who rescues a person or a people from slavery, danger, or oppression. In Acts 7:35, Moses is called a "liberator" because God sent him to deliver the Israelites from slavery in Egypt: he led them to freedom.
2. The term also refers to one who redeems, who saves in a spiritual sense. There is the idea of paying a price to obtain someone's release, as one redeems a prisoner. This is why this word naturally applies to the one who saves us from sin and death.
G3086.origine: The word comes from the root λυτρόω (lytroô), "to redeem, to liberate for a price." This root evokes the ancient image of redemption: just as money is paid to free a slave or a prisoner, the root conveys the idea of purchasing freedom. In the Greek Old Testament, the Hebrew word גָּאַל (gaal), "to redeem, to avenge," is often rendered by this family of Greek words. God is the great liberator of Israel, particularly from the Egyptian yoke.
G3086.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 7:35, where Stephen addresses the crowd in Jerusalem. He describes Moses as the liberator whom God sent long ago to save Israel. Stephen contrasts Moses' glorious mission (sent by God as leader and liberator) with the rejection he faced from the people. The context shows that this title emphasizes Moses' prominent role in the history of Israel's salvation.
G3086.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to recognize that only God can truly liberate us. Moses was a temporary earthly liberator, but in Jesus Christ, we find the ultimate Liberator, the one who redeems us from sin and grants us eternal freedom. Understanding Moses as a "liberator" helps to see how the Old Testament points to the final work of deliverance that Jesus accomplishes.

sens: an object designed to hold and illuminate with a lamp or light
a piece of furniture used in worship in the Tabernacle and the Temple
G3087.detail:
1. A candelabrum is a support or utensil that holds a lit lamp to provide light. In Jesus' teachings (Matthew 5:15, Mark 4:21, Luke 8:16, 11:33), the candelabrum represents the place where a lamp is set—not under a bushel or under a bed, but prominently on the candelabrum, so that its light shines throughout the house. It is a simple, familiar everyday object.
2. The candelabrum is also the sacred piece of furniture that was in the Tabernacle: in Hebrews 9:2, it is listed among the holy objects of the "holy place," alongside the table and the showbread. It is a liturgical utensil, crafted carefully according to divine prescriptions.
G3087.origine: The Greek word λυχνία (luchnia) literally means what receives or holds a light: it is derived from λῦχος (lychos, "lamp"). It is a common form of Greek. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses the word מְנוֹרָה (ménorah) to refer to the candelabrum of the sanctuary. The context of the Greek translations of the Old Testament shows that λυχνία translates this Hebrew term, thus linking the two testaments in the same cultic reality.
G3087.emploi: The word appears eleven times in the New Testament. It is used first in the literal and everyday sense in the three Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke): Jesus uses it to teach that spiritual light should not remain hidden but should shine openly. In Hebrews 9:2, the word refers to the golden candelabrum of the historical Tabernacle, a key element of Levitical worship. In Revelation (1:12-13, 1:20, 2:1, 2:5, 11:4), John uses the candelabrum symbolically: the seven golden candelabra represent the seven churches of Asia, and the candelabrum also appears with the two witnesses. The vision of the Resurrected One surrounded by the candelabra shows that the churches are homes of divine light. The expression "to remove the candelabrum" (Revelation 2:5) means to take away a church's function as a shining witness.
G3087.portee: For the believer, the candelabrum illustrates that faith is not a private matter: it must shine visibly to illuminate others. Jesus calls his disciples not to hide their spiritual light. Furthermore, the image of the candelabrum in Revelation reminds us that local churches are witnesses of Christ in the world; they have a responsibility to maintain this luminous mission. It is a call to courageous visibility and spiritual vigilance.

sens: A portable small object, fueled by oil, that produces light
A container or support placed on a candelabrum to illuminate a house
Light that illuminates or guides
Symbol of one who testifies, who enlightens others with their message
Symbol of insight and heart attentiveness
Figure of divine power and glory
G3088.detail:
1. A lamp is a small object that can be carried from one place to another, fueled by oil, and that burns to provide light (Luke 15:8: a woman lights a lamp to find a lost coin in her house).

2. This lamp is placed on a candelabrum or support so that it shines better and illuminates the whole house (Matthew 5:15: "a lamp is not lit to be put under a bushel, but it is placed on a candelabrum").

3. The lamp becomes an image of what guides and illuminates (2 Peter 1:19: the prophetic word is "a lamp shining in a dark place").

4. Jesus calls John the Baptist "a lamp" (John 5:35), because he burned and shone in testifying to the truth.

5. The eye is called "the lamp of the body" (Matthew 6:22): it illuminates our understanding and perception of things.

6. Ultimately, the Lamb himself is the lamp of the heavenly city (Revelation 21:23), his glory replacing all created illumination.
G3088.origine: The Greek word for "lamp" comes from a root that evokes what burns and shines. In Hebrew, the term "nir" was used for lamp and light. It is a word rooted in daily life: every house needed lamps for illumination. The Greek word thus translates a concrete object from the ancient world, as indispensable as flame to conquer darkness.
G3088.emploi: The word "lamp" appears 14 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke and Revelation. It is used first in the literal sense: a lamp is lit, placed on a candelabrum (Matthew 5:15, Mark 4:21, Luke 11:33, Luke 15:8). But the image quickly becomes symbolic: John the Baptist is a "lamp that burns and shines" (John 5:35) for those who believe in him. The disciples are urged to have their "lamps lit," ready to welcome the bridegroom (Luke 12:35). The eye is the "lamp of the body" (Matthew 6:22, Luke 11:34): if it is pure, the whole body sees clearly. Prophecy is a lamp in darkness (2 Peter 1:19). Finally, the Lamb in the new heaven replaces every lamp (Revelation 21:23, 22:5), for his light surpasses all.
G3088.portee: This image shows the importance of light in God's plan: what illuminates is fragile, localized, dependent on a source (faith, testimony, prophetic word), but it is what allows us to see clearly. It reminds the believer that they are not here by chance: if a lamp is lit, it is to shine for "all who are in the house" (Matthew 5:15). Everyone has received a light, a truth to share. It is also an invitation to examine our own hearts: is my eye, my intention, my insight directed toward God, or clouded by selfishness?

sens: To detach or untie an attached object, a bound person
To free an animal from its tether
To release a person from captivity or slavery
To annul, break, or render void (a law, a commandment, a covenant)
To break or reduce to pieces (an object, a structure)
To destroy, annihilate, or abolish (a power, a work)
G3089.detail:
1. To loose primarily means to remove the ties that attach something: to detach a sandal, to undo a knot. It is the simplest physical action, as when Peter is asked to loose the cords of his shoes (Mark 1:7).
2. To free an animal from its tether means to allow it to move freely. Jesus permits the untethering of the donkey and its colt on the Sabbath (Luke 13:15), showing that a bound creature can be liberated even on that day.
3. To release a person who is imprisoned or enslaved means to remove their chains. Jesus commands that Lazarus be loosed, wrapped in strips of linen (John 11:44), and the apostles are loosed from prison (Acts 22:30).
4. When speaking of a law or commandment, to loose means to annul or break it. Jesus heals on the Sabbath without violating this law, as healing carries more weight (John 7:23); the Pharisee who looses the least commandment will be the least in the kingdom (Matthew 5:19).
5. To break or destroy a physical structure: the ship breaks on the rocks (Acts 27:41); on the last day, the heavens will dissolve in fire (2 Peter 3:12).
6. To annihilate an enemy or evil power: Jesus came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8); Satan will be loosed before his final condemnation (Revelation 20:3, 7).
G3089.origine: The Greek verb λύω comes from an Indo-European root meaning "to break, to open." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates פָּתַח (pâtach, to open) or נָתַר (nâtar, to loose). The word has a concrete image: that of someone undoing a tie to free what was held. This idea of "liberation" through loosing naturally extends to annulling a law or destroying a power.
G3089.emploi: The verb λύω appears 41 times in the New Testament, primarily in John, Mark, and Luke. It is first used in the literal sense: to untie animals (Mark 11:2, Luke 19:30), to loose prisoners (Acts 22:30). Very quickly, it takes on figurative meanings: to annul a law (Matthew 5:19, John 5:18), to break moral or spiritual bonds (John 11:44, 1 Corinthians 7:27 regarding marriage). In Paul and Peter, it describes the destruction of the structures of the current world (Acts 2:24, 2 Peter 3:10-12). In John and Revelation, it expresses the annihilation of the works of evil and of the devil himself (1 John 3:8, Revelation 20:3, 7). The context determines the nuance: physical, legal, or eschatological.
G3089.portee: This word reminds Christians that liberation, in all its forms, is the work of Christ: liberation from sin, from the moral burden of the Law, from fear and death. It also invites discernment about what should be loosed (the structures of sin, the chains of the wicked) from what should remain firm (the word of God, His covenant). For each believer, to loose sometimes means accepting to be delivered, and sometimes consenting to let go of what God wants to break.

sens: Grandmother of the apostle Timothy
G3090.detail: Lois is the maternal grandmother of Timothy. She is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the letter that Paul addresses to his young collaborator Timothy. Paul reminds Timothy that his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice possessed sincere faith, and he is convinced that this faith also dwells in Timothy himself (2 Timothy 1:5).
G3090.origine: The name Lois is Greek and means "desirable" or "pleasant." It is a Greek feminine name borne by a woman of Jewish faith, as Paul speaks of her faith in Jesus Christ. No notable Hebrew-Greek etymology applies to this proper name.
G3090.emploi: Lois appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Timothy 1:5. Paul writes to Timothy to encourage him to cultivate his faith. He then mentions the example of the sincere faith that first dwelled in his grandmother Lois, then in his mother Eunice, and now remains in Timothy himself. It is a touching testimony of the transmission of faith within a family across generations.
G3090.portee: The memory of Lois reminds us that the Christian faith is often passed down from one generation to the next, and that the example of the elders nourishes the faith of the young. Timothy, raised in an atmosphere of trust in Jesus Christ, received a precious inheritance: this shows the importance of the role of women and mothers in the spiritual education of their children and grandchildren.

sens: Nephew of Abraham, living in Sodom
Righteous man delivered from divine judgment
Witness to the condemnation of Sodom and Gomorrah
G3091.detail:
1. Lot is the son of Haran and the nephew of Abraham. He chose to settle in Sodom, in the Jordan Valley, where he prospered but found himself in the midst of a city given over to evil and immorality (Luke 17:28-29).
2. Jesus designates him as a righteous man, deeply distressed by the unrestrained conduct of those around him (2 Peter 2:7). Although he chose to live among the wicked, his heart remained separate from their practices.
3. His story embodies God's judgment on sin: the day he had to flee Sodom, a rain of fire and brimstone destroyed the city and all its inhabitants (Luke 17:29). Jesus cites his example to warn that judgment will come unexpectedly, and He exhorts not to forget the warning given to Lot's wife (Luke 17:32).
G3091.origine: The name Lot (Hebrew לוֹט, Lôt) appears in Genesis as a key member of Abraham's family. His story, detailed in Genesis 12-19, shows how he followed Abraham in his migration, then separated to seek more fertile lands. The New Testament takes him as an example of the contrast between the righteous living amidst evil and the divine judgment that strikes impiety.
G3091.emploi: Lot appears four times in the New Testament, always in the context of the judgment of Sodom. Luke 17:28-29 cites him when Jesus teaches about the last days: the ordinary life of the inhabitants of Sodom (eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building) came to an end the day Lot left, when the fire from heaven consumed the city. Luke 17:32 calls to remember Lot's wife, turned into a pillar of salt for looking back. In 2 Peter 2:7, the apostle refers to him as "righteous," showing that despite his life in Sodom, his conscience remained sensitive to the surrounding wickedness. These uses make Lot a warning and an example of divine deliverance.
G3091.portee: Lot's story teaches that God's justice is exercised even on those who seem to prosper amidst evil, and that He delivers the righteous from the judgment that strikes impiety. It invites the believer to examine their heart: can one remain faithful to God when living surrounded by sin? Finally, the warning "remember Lot's wife" calls for radical obedience to God's judgment, without nostalgia for the condemned world.

sens: Character in the genealogy of Jesus mentioned in the Gospel of Luke
G3092.detail: Maath is an ancestor of Jesus according to the genealogy presented by Luke in chapter 3. He is listed among the direct ancestors of the Lord, situated between Mattathias and Shem (Luke 3:26). This genealogy traces back to Adam and shows how Jesus fits into the history of God's people.
G3092.origine: The name Maath is of Hebrew origin. It appears only once in the New Testament. It is found in the genealogy traced by Luke, which partially differs from that given by Matthew, reflecting distinct genealogical traditions in the early Church.
G3092.emploi: Maath appears only once in the Bible, in Luke 3:26, in the genealogy of Jesus presented immediately after the Lord's baptism. Luke enumerates the ancestors of Jesus back to Adam, emphasizing the universality of the salvation brought by Christ. Maath simply represents one of these links in the genealogical chain.

sens: Place located on the shore of the Sea of Galilee
G3093.detail: 1. Magadan (also called Magdala in some manuscripts) is a place situated on the shores of the Sea of Galilee in the Holy Land. The Hebrew name means "tower" or "fortress." In Matthew 15:39, after miraculously feeding four thousand people in the wilderness, Jesus dismisses the crowd, boards a boat, and heads to the region of Magadan — a movement that shows his constant movement around the lake with his disciples.
G3093.origine: The word comes from the Aramaic מַגְדְֺּלָא (magdelâ), which corresponds to the Hebrew מִגְדָּל (migdal), meaning "tower" or "fortified structure." It is a geographical place name, not a common word. Ancient scribes transmitted this name in two slightly different forms — Magadan and Magdala — which explains the variations in Greek manuscripts, particularly in Matthew 15:39 and Mark 8:10.
G3093.emploi: Magadan appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 15:39, where it is mentioned as a coastal region to which Jesus heads after a miracle. Mark 8:10 apparently refers to the same place under the name of Dalmanoutha, although some ancient manuscripts propose other variants. The exact location remains difficult to identify with certainty on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, despite the efforts of biblical geographers.

sens: woman from Magdala, a town in Galilee
disciple of Jesus who followed and supported him
woman in the gospels freed from demons by Jesus
G3094.detail:
1. Mary Magdalene is a woman from Magdala, a small port on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. The name "of Magdala" simply indicates her city of origin, just as one might say "Peter of Bethsaida" or "Philip of Bethsaida" (John 1:44). It was a common way to designate someone by their place of origin.

2. She is one of the women who followed Jesus in Galilee and provided for his needs (Luke 8:2). She is mentioned in all four gospels as a witness to the crucifixion, the burial, and as the first to meet the resurrected Jesus (Mark 16:9, John 20:1).

3. According to Mark 16:9, Jesus had cast seven demons out of her, which marks both her deliverance and Jesus' power over the forces of evil. This profound liberation likely motivated her devotion to Jesus.
G3094.origine: The name comes from Magdala (in Hebrew Migdal, "tower"), a town on the Galilean coast. In Greek, the adjective Magdalēnē, "of Magdala," is added to the name Maria to form "Maria Magdalēnē." The suffix -ēnē always indicates belonging to a place.
G3094.emploi: Mary Magdalene appears in all four gospels (12 occurrences in total). She is first mentioned in Luke 8:2 as a woman from whom Jesus had cast out seven demons, among those who followed him. She reappears at three decisive moments: at the cross (Matthew 27:56, Mark 15:40, John 19:25), at the tomb where she looks to see where Jesus is laid (Matthew 27:61, Mark 15:47), and at the resurrection where she seeks the body of Jesus (Matthew 28:1, Mark 16:1, Luke 24:10, John 20:1). Mark and John give Mary Magdalene particular importance: she is the first to whom the resurrected Jesus appears (Mark 16:9, John 20:18).
G3094.portee: Mary Magdalene exemplifies faithfulness to the end: she does not disappear at the cross or at the burial, unlike many disciples. She also shows that Jesus attracts and transforms those who need him, regardless of their past condition. Finally, she is honored by the evangelists as a witness to the resurrection, reminding us that the Gospel entrusts women with a central mission in the history of salvation.

sens: The art of the Magi, a people known for mysterious and supernatural practices
Practice of occult powers, witchcraft
Set of tricks, feats that astonish and fascinate
G3095.detail: 1. The word originally refers to the science and practices of the Magi, a people known in antiquity for mysterious rituals and operations reputed to be supernatural. 2. By extension, it applies to any witchcraft or occult practice — that is, the exercise of hidden powers, contrary to the natural order. 3. In a broader sense, it also describes tricks and feats that produce wonder and fascination in those who observe them, as when Simon the magician in Acts 8:11 amazed the inhabitants with his acts of magic.
G3095.origine: The word comes from μάγος (magos), which designates a Magus — a member of a Persian priestly caste known for astrology, rituals, and esoteric practices. The root evokes the idea of hidden power, secret and impressive knowledge. It is a word of Eastern origin, which has retained its connection with the reputation of the Magi in Greek and Western thought.
G3095.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:11, where it qualifies the activity of Simon, a magician from Samaria who had captivated the population with astonishing wonders. Simon presented himself as a great figure by performing acts of magic, which granted him a large following among his contemporaries — until Philip came to proclaim the Gospel with authentic signs and wonders. The term highlights the contrast between false power, based on deceptive fascination, and the real power of God.
G3095.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that magic — whether occult or merely spectacular — can seduce and captivate, but it remains a hollow imitation of true divine power. The story of Simon shows that even those who are impressed by magic can recognize the superiority of God's word and acts when they encounter it. It serves as a warning against false promises and deceptive tricks.

sens: To practice acts of magic, witchcraft, or divination
To use formulas, rituals, or powers purportedly supernatural to impress or deceive
G3096.detail:
1. The verb designates the activity of one who presents themselves as a magician or sorcerer: they perform spectacular acts, make ritual gestures, or pronounce words believed to have hidden power over visible realities. In Acts 8:9, Simon claims to "exercise magic" in Samaria and fascinates the people with his performances.
2. More broadly, it refers to practicing an art supposedly supernatural, often to gain prestige, influence, or money. Biblical magic is presented as a deception or a counterfeit of true divine power.
G3096.origine: The word comes from the Greek « magos » (μάγος), which designates the mage or magician — initially the Zoroastrian priests of Persia, reputedly skilled in occult sciences, and later any practitioner of magic or witchcraft. The verb « mageuō » is directly formed from this noun: it means "to act as a magus," that is, to engage in magic. It is a well-established word in the Greek of ancient authors (Euripides, Plutarch) and in the Greek of Hellenized Jews.
G3096.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:9. Simon of Samaria used it to deceive the people. The context shows that magic was perceived as a means of seduction and false power: it fascinates ("caused amazement"), it grants influence, but it has no real foundation before God. In contrast, the early Church recognizes in Peter and John the true power of God, which operates not through tricks but through faith and the name of Jesus.
G3096.portee: For the Christian, this word serves as a reminder that magic and witchcraft are seductions, counterfeits of divine power. They attract through the spectacular and the mysterious, but they deliver no true power. The Bible invites the believer to turn away from these practices and to seek only the power of God, which acts without deception and truly transforms.

sens: Member of a Median priestly caste, specialist in occult sciences and astrology
One who practices magic, witchcraft, or occult arts
G3097.detail:
1. The Magi from the East who visit Jesus in Bethlehem (Matthew 2:1, 7, 16) belong to a priestly caste of Median origin, recognized in the ancient world for their knowledge of astrology and mysterious sciences. They were learned men, dignitaries and scholars, capable of interpreting celestial signs—the appearance of the star led them to Jesus. King Herod consults them and treats them with respect, although he ultimately sees them as rivals.

2. A Magus can also be a magician or sorcerer, someone who claims to master the occult arts and supernatural powers to exert influence over others. Elymas in Acts 13:6, 8 is described as a false prophet who uses magic to deceive and turn people away from the Christian faith. The contrast is striking: while the Magi of Bethlehem seek the truth and submit to Jesus, Elymas opposes the Gospel through his tricks.
G3097.origine: The Greek word μάγος comes from the Median language and originally refers to the priests and sages of Media (an ancient kingdom in the Middle East). The Greeks borrowed this term to designate this respected caste. In Hebrew, the underlying word is אַשָּׁף (ashaf), which means diviner or enchanter. The word retains this dual meaning: on one side, the scholars and observers of the stars; on the other, the charlatans who claim to manipulate hidden forces.
G3097.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the New Testament. Three occurrences in Matthew 2 concern the Magi from the East who come to worship the newborn Jesus: they are dignified figures, learned in astronomy and astrology, who recognize the messianic sign. Two occurrences in Acts 13 refer to Elymas, a Jewish magician in Paphos who tries to seduce the proconsul with occult tricks and opposes Paul. One mention in Acts 8:9 (in the source definition) refers to Simon the magician. The meaning thus varies: noble and seeker of truth among the Magi of Bethlehem, fraudulent and hostile in the cases of Elymas and Simon.
G3097.portee: The Magi of Bethlehem illustrate how God reveals Himself even to the learned of the pagan world and how the sincerity of the heart—the desire to find the truth—leads to Jesus. Their example encourages the reader to recognize that God speaks to all peoples. In contrast, Elymas and Simon show the danger of occult practices that claim supernatural power: they oppose the Gospel and deceive souls. The Bible thus marks a clear distinction between true wisdom (which leads to Jesus) and false magic (which misleads).

sens: Territory or people of the ancient world, associated with Gog, often located to the north
G3098.detail: 1. Magog refers to a people or territory mentioned in the Old Testament as a son or descendant of Japheth (Genesis 10:2). In Revelation, Magog reappears alongside Gog as an enemy power of the last days: "And he will go out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth, Gog and Magog, to gather them for battle" (Revelation 20:8). It is a biblical image of the final rebellion against the people of God, gathered by Satan after a thousand years, before his ultimate defeat.
G3098.origine: Magog comes from the Hebrew מָגוֹג (Magog), mentioned as early as Genesis 10:2 among the sons of Japheth. The name is used as is in Greek in the New Testament. Its exact etymology remains debated, but it designates a people or territory of the ancient world, often associated with regions in the northern Caucasus or Scythia. Revelation links Magog to Gog, the leader of this eschatological power.
G3098.emploi: Magog appears only once in the New Testament: in Revelation 20:8, at the time of the final revolt of the nations against God. John draws on the imagery from the Old Testament (Ezekiel 38-39, where Gog rules over the land of Magog) to symbolically describe the forces of evil gathered at the end of times. It is not so much a precise geographical description as an eschatological enemy power, a symbol of the ultimate rebellion against the Kingdom of God.
G3098.portee: Magog reminds Christians that the Bible speaks of spiritual struggles that fit within an arc of history that stretches from creation to the end of time. This name also shows that Satan never gives up: even after the final judgment of the devil, he attempts to rally the nations against God. It is an invitation to vigilance and trust in the ultimate victory of Christ.

sens: Son of Abraham and Keturah
Arab people descended from Midian
Region of Arabia where this people lived
G3099.detail:
1. Midian is one of the sons that Abraham had with his concubine Keturah after the death of Sarah (Genesis 25:2). From this son, a lineage was born.
2. The name Midian also refers to the Arab people descended from this son, an important tribe of the Arabian desert mentioned in the Old Testament alongside other peoples (Psalms 83:9).
3. The land of Midian is the region where this people lived, a territory in Arabia. It is there that Moses fled after killing an Egyptian, and where he met Jethro and married his daughter Zipporah (Exodus 2:15; Acts 7:29).
G3099.origine: The Hebrew name מִדְיָן (Midyân) refers both to the son of Abraham and the people descended from him, a common practice in the Bible where the name of an ancestor becomes that of his entire clan. The Greek faithfully retains this Hebrew name. Midian represents one of the great Arab families of antiquity, established in the Arabian desert.
G3099.emploi: Midian appears rarely in the New Testament, only in Acts where the apostle Peter, citing the Old Testament, recalls how Moses "went to dwell in the land of Midian" after leaving Egypt (Acts 7:29). It is a historical reference to show how God guided Moses before his calling at Sinai. In the Old Testament, the Midianites are presented as desert nomads with whom Israel often interacted, sometimes as neighbors, sometimes as adversaries.
